III. Thanksgiving for Conversion and Intercession for Understanding (1:15–23)

A. Thanksgiving for Faith and Love, and Intercession for Illumination (1:15–19)

B. God’s Great Power Displayed in Christ and for the Church (1:20–23)


B. God’s Great Power Displayed in Christ and for the Church (1:20–23)

To his thanksgiving and intercessory prayer report, Paul now attaches a lengthy relative clause (vv. 20–21) and a new sentence (vv. 22–22), which explain how God put his mighty strength into effect for believers. The entire section, therefore, functions as an explanation of the third and final “what” clause of Paul’s intercessory prayer report. In this third clause, Paul has just told his readers how he prays that God might, by his Spirit, cause them to know “what is the surpassing greatness of his power for us who believe” (v. 19). Now Paul explains the immense proportions of that power and how it is applied to those who believe. God’s power raised Christ from the dead and seated him, victorious, at God’s right hand, with all enemy forces conquered and beneath Christ’s feet (1:20–22a). God has also given Christ to the church in his capacity as victorious, authoritative head over all these forces (1:22b–23).

This small paragraph provides an important function in the design of the letter. At the level of the letter’s argument, it spells out more precisely how God has shown his great power and how he has used these manifestations of his power for the benefit of believers. At the level of the letter’s epistolary form, it provides a transition from the letter’s prayer section into the letter’s main theological discussion in chapters 2 and 3. It does this in a way so compatible with the prayer report, however, that we are not surprised to find Paul returning to his prayers in 3:1 and 14.

The progress of thought in the passage is clear, although its grammatical structure is slightly disorganized and at places ambiguous. Grammatically, the first part of the passage is closely linked with the third “what” clause (1:19) of the intercessory prayer report by the relative pronoun “which” (ἥν, hēn) and so continues the long sentence that began the thanksgiving and intercessory prayer report section in verse 15. A new sentence does not begin until verse 22. The expansion of the third “what” clause of the prayer report is so long, however, that the NA27 and most English translations place a period at the end of verse 19 and start a new sentence, or even a new paragraph, at verse 20. This way of construing the structure correctly recognizes that the third “what” clause of the prayer report announces Paul’s primary concern in the report itself, and an important topic in the letter, a topic that Paul immediately explains in more detail in the new section. What is lost in organizing the sentence this way is the run-on quality of Paul’s language and therefore the emotional engagement and emphasis that this characteristic of Paul’s style in Ephesians communicates.

The loose connection between grammatical form and logical argument continues in verses 22–23, where Paul does begin a new sentence, albeit connected with the preceding clause with καί (kai, and). The thought, however, simply continues that of verses 20–21. Not until the second half of verse 22 does Paul introduce a new thought and bring the section full circle back to the announcement of his theme in verse 19. The grammatical structure of this new thought (“and he gave him”), however, is identical to the grammatical structure of the first half of the verse (“and he subjected all things”). In other words, Paul does not carefully match the flow of his thought with the grammatical structure of his language: primary and subordinate thoughts are not correlated with main and subordinate clauses. Moreover, Paul concludes the section with one of the most difficult clauses in the letter to interpret, variously translated “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (NRSV), “the fullness of the one who fills all things in every way” (NAB; cf. TNIV), “the fullness of him who is filled, all in all” (NJB), and “the fullness of him who is filling the universe in all its parts” (REB).

For all the ambiguity at the level of the grammar, however, the basic thought of the passage is not only clear but also highly organized and coherent. Paul’s third “what” clause in the intercessory prayer report stated that God has used his power for the benefit of those who believe the gospel. In verses 20–22a, Paul shows precisely how God has used that power. He has raised Christ from the dead and seated him at God’s right hand, far above all inimical heavenly powers. These powers lie conquered beneath Christ’s feet.

The terminology Paul uses to communicate this truth is a skillful blend of language from Israel’s Scriptures and language from the Greco-Roman environment that surrounded Paul’s readers. Paul uses the language of Pss. 110:1 (109:1 LXX) and 8:6 (8:7 MT, LXX) to say that just as “the LORD” in Ps. 110 gave a military victory to the king and in Ps. 8 subjected all creation to human beings, so God has given his anointed king Jesus, the Messiah, victory over all forces ranged against him.[1] When Paul lists the heavenly powers that God has conquered for his Messiah, he uses terms that in the religious environment of his readers typically referred to the gods who were thought to control the fate of human beings and the destiny of nations. Fear of such powers was common, as was the belief that honoring the deities who controlled the fates of nations could bring social and individual prosperity. Paul prays that his readers might understand that God has given the Christ, in whom they believed when they embraced the gospel, victory over all such powers. This is specifically how God has displayed “the surpassing greatness of his power” and “the might of his strength” that Paul mentioned in verse 19.

Paul also said in verse 19, however, that God uses his power “for us who believe,” and so in verses 22b–23 he explains in fuller detail what this means. The headship over all things, which God gave to Christ when he raised him and seated him high above his enemies, is a headship that he exercises for the church, the congregation of those who have believed the gospel, wherever they might be. The church, Paul says, is Christ’s body, and since all things—especially all inimical powers—are subject to Christ, they are also subject to the church. The great power that God exerted in Christ to make him victorious over his enemies, therefore, is also a power God has exerted on behalf of the church.



Exegesis and Exposition

20. . . which [effect] he effected in the Messiah by raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand in the heavenly places, 21high above all rule and authority and power and lordship and every name that is named not only in this age, but also in the one to come, 22aand he subjected all things under his feet 22band gave him as ⌜head⌝ over all things to the church 23which is, in truth, his body, that which is full of the One who is continuously and completely filled.

[1:20–22a] In 1:20–22a, Paul illustrates the effect of God’s great power by reminding his readers of God’s resurrection and exaltation of the Messiah. In these powerful acts, God gave his anointed king the victory over all his enemies. Paul begins with the relative pronoun ἥν, whose antecedent is the noun ἐνέργεια (energeia, effect) in verse 19, as the cognate verb ἐνήργησεν (enērgēsen, he effected) shows. God put into effect his effective power in the Messiah when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand.[2]

Here Paul alludes to Ps. 110:1 MT, Eng. (109:1 LXX), and specifically to the reference in that psalm to the king’s exaltation to God’s right hand (v. 1a). The psalm probably played a role in first-century debates about the identity of the Messiah even beyond Christian circles, as Jesus’s use of it in debates with his opponents and at his Jewish trial implies (Moritz 1996a: 16–17﻿).[3] Quotations of and allusions to it appear frequently in the NT, where the main interest is the exaltation of Jesus to God’s right hand (Hay 1973: 163–66). Usually in those texts the emphasis lies on the vindication of Jesus after his crucifixion, or on his highly exalted status as God’s vice regent (Acts 2:33–35; Col. 3:1; Heb. 1:3–4, 13; 8:1; Rev. 5:1, 7; cf. Rom. 8:34).

Those connotations may be present for Paul here, but his chief concern in alluding to the psalm lies not in the location of the king at God’s right hand, but in God’s defeat of the king’s enemies in the second half of the verse (Ps. 110:1b [109:1b LXX]), the part of the psalm to which Paul does not explicitly allude.[4] Paul implies this idea in the next two prepositional phrases, and then he states it explicitly in verse 22a, using the language of Ps. 8:6 (8:7 MT, LXX) rather than Ps. 110:1b.

He says that Christ was seated at God’s right hand ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις (en tois epouraniois, in the heavenly places), an expression that we have already examined in the comments on 1:3. The phrase is a blanket term describing the “dimension” in which all spiritual powers exist, whether good, as in 1:3 (cf. 2:6), or inimical to God’s purposes, as in 6:12 (cf. 3:10; W. H. Harris 1991: 86, quoting Hanson 1980: 138).

Paul also says that Christ was seated at God’s right hand ὑπεράνω (hyperanō, high above) a long list of powerful beings: πάσης ἀρχῆς καὶ ἐξουσίας καὶ δυνάμεως καὶ κυριότητος καὶ παντὸς ὀνόματος ὀνομαζομένου (pasēs archēs kai exousias kai dynameōs kai kyriotētos kai pantos onomatos onomazomenou, all rule and authority and power and lordship and every name that is named). The position of the Messiah ὑπεράνω these powers in a context where Ps. 110:1 is in the air shows that they are inimical powers and that God has given the Messiah Jesus victory over them (cf. 6:12).

As the introduction to the commentary explains, Paul probably included among these powers not only the demonic forces that many people in western Asia Minor during this period tried to control through magic (Arnold 1989; 1995), but also the alliance between present earthly political rulers and the deities of the transcendent realm. This becomes even more likely when Paul adds the comment that Christ’s victory is effective οὐ μόνον ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι (ou monon en tō aiōni toutō alla kai en tō mellonti, not only in this age, but also in the one to come). Many interpreters correctly draw attention to the Jewish nature of the idiom Paul uses here (e.g., Robinson 1904: 121; Lincoln 1990: 65). Jewish and early Christian literature often distinguishes between the present age and the age to come.[5] Paul, too, frequently speaks of the present age elsewhere in his letters, although this is the only place in the Pauline corpus where the full contrast between the two ages is explicitly expressed.[6]

Since the eschatology of Ephesians emphasizes the present realization of God’s triumph over evil (1:3; 2:6, 13; 3:9–10), and since Paul has just spoken of this triumph in language that emphasizes its completeness (1:20–21a), a number of interpreters have concluded that Paul (or the author) does not mean by this phrase that there is any coming age in which Christ will continue to exercise authority. He is using traditional language, they argue, only to emphasize the completeness of Christ’s triumph (e.g., Lindemann 1975: 210–11; Schnackenburg 1991: 78–79; Best 1998: 174). In response, a number of other commentators have observed that although the Paul of Ephesians does lay special emphasis on the presence of God’s triumph over evil in Christ’s resurrection and exaltation to God’s right hand, he still affirms that this triumph will be completed only in the future (1:10, 14; 2:7; 4:30; 5:27; 6:8, 11–12; O’Brien 1999: 143; Hoehner 2002: 281–82; cf. Sellin 2008: 144).

It may be important for understanding Paul’s intentions in penning this phrase to keep in mind the Greco-Roman context of his language about time, both here and elsewhere in the letter. Coins, statuary, reliefs, inscriptions, and the calendar of Asia tempted Paul’s readers to think that time was organized around the imperial authority of Rome and that Rome’s authority was eternal. One Ephesian house, recently excavated, featured the graffito, “Rome, the ruler of all, your power will never die.” A decree of the city of Assos, issued in AD 37, speaks of “the most pleasant age for humanity that is now present” (τοῦ ἡδίστου ἀνθρώποις αἰῶνος νῦν ἐνεστῶτος, tou hēdistou anthrōpois aiōnos nyn enestōtos).[7] In a culture where such statements were prevalent, Paul reminds his readers that God has organized time around Christ (1:10) and that Christ holds supreme authority over all inimical powers both now and forever (1:21b).

The challenge to all powers that either are opposed to God’s people or claim an authority that belongs only to the Messiah continues in verse 22a. Here, just as he did in 1 Cor. 15:25–27, and like some other early Christian writers (1 Pet. 3:22; Heb. 1:3, 13; 2:6–8), Paul supplements his allusion to Ps. 110:1 (109:1 LXX) with a paraphrase of Ps. 8:6 (8:7 MT, LXX).[8] It is possible that Paul simply followed an early Christian exegetical tradition that sometimes linked Ps. 110:1 (109:1 LXX) with Ps. 8:6 (8:7) and did not have the wider contexts of these psalms or their subject matter in mind when he alluded to them (e.g., Abbott 1897: 43; Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 65; Lincoln 1982: 41–42).

In light of what we have seen of the religious and political environment in which Paul wrote Ephesians, however, Paul may have been thinking of Ps. 8 in its entirety when he alluded to Ps. 8:6 here, although his point is different than that of the psalm. Psalm 8 (NRSV) portrays human beings as “a little lower than God” (v. 5a), “crowned . . . with glory and honor” (v. 5b), and given “dominion” over God’s creation (v. 6)—in other words, as exercising a divinely given sovereignty over all the earth. The kind of linkage between divine and human rule that the psalm found between human beings and God (cf. Gen. 1:26), and that many people in Roman Asia believed Augustus and his successors exemplified, Paul finds instead in the Messiah Jesus.[9]

[1:22b] Paul’s thought now comes full circle, back to verse 19 (Lincoln 1990: 67). There he told his readers of his prayers that God would open the eyes of their hearts so that they might understand the great magnitude of the power that God had exerted “for us who believe.” After expanding on the greatness of God’s power in verses 20–22a, Paul now tells his readers how God has used this power for the advantage of the company of believers, a group that Paul now calls “the church”: καὶ αὐτὸν ἔδωκεν κεφαλὴν ὑπὲρ πάντα τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ (kai auton edōken kephalēn hyper panta tē ekklēsia, and he gave him as head over all things to the church).

The term ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia) referred primarily to a political assembly in ancient Greek literature (e.g., Aristotle, Pol. 3.14 [3.1285a.11]; Herodotus, Hist. 3.142), and this made it a natural choice for the LXX translators when they needed a word to refer to “the assembly [קָהָל, qāhāl] of the LORD” (Deut. 23:2; 1 Chron. 28:8; Mic. 2:5), “the assembly of God” (Neh. 13:1), or “the assembly of the Most High” (Sir. 24:2). Since Paul did not think of the church as a political assembly, and ἐκκλησία was not the obvious term for a society or club in the Roman world (Wilken 1984: 33), he probably reflects the use of the word in the LXX. He seems to have thought of the multiethnic church of his own time as, in some sense, continuous with the “assembly of the LORD” in Israel’s Scriptures (1 Thess. 2:14; 2 Thess. 1:4; 1 Cor. 1:2; 10:32; 11:16; 15:9; Gal. 1:13; 2 Cor. 1:1).[10] Although that thought will become more prominent in Eph. 5:25–27, it is not his concern here (see the comments on 5:27). The context shows that when Paul speaks of “the church” in 1:22b, he means those who have heard and believed the gospel (1:13, 19), “the collection [σύλλογος, syllogos] of the faithful,” as Theodoret puts it (R. Hill 2001: 2.237).

Here and elsewhere in Ephesians, Paul uses ἐκκλησία in the sense of the universal church, a meaning that is especially prominent in the later letters of the Pauline corpus, whose Pauline authorship is disputed.[11] The more general use of the term does find precedent in Paul’s earlier and undisputed correspondence (1 Cor. 10:32; 15:9; Gal. 1:13; Phil. 3:6), however, and a change in the nature of Paul’s ministry in the later letters rather than a change to pseudonymous authorship probably best accounts for the increase in general uses of the term.[12]

Some interpreters, apparently startled by the notion that Christ is described here as a gift to the church, have translated ἔδωκεν (edōken, he gave) as if it were ἔθηκεν (ethēken, he appointed) and rendered the phrase “he made him head” or something similar.[13] It is possible that δίδωμι carries this meaning on rare occasion, but the standard examples of this meaning are all debatable (Num. 14:4; Acts 13:20; Barn. 14.7; Isa. 42:6; BDAG 242). This makes it far more likely that Paul used the verb in its normal way here to say that God gave Christ to the church.[14]

Although it is unusual within the NT to see Christ described as a gift to the church (Muddiman 2001: 91–92), it is reasonably easy to understand what Paul is saying, especially if we take seriously his qualification of this thought with the phrase κεφαλὴν ὑπὲρ πάντα (kephalēn hyper panta, as head over all things). God has given Christ to the church in Christ’s capacity as head over all things. Paul has just shown his readers that God worked powerfully in Christ’s resurrection and exaltation to give him victory over all inimical forces in the heavenly realms, and he has just summarized this description with a paraphrase of Ps. 8:6 that speaks of God subjecting πάντα (panta, all things) under Christ’s πόδες (podes, feet). He now moves from feet to head: if all things are beneath Christ’s feet, then he is the head of all things.[15] Moreover (and this is Paul’s main point), he is the head of all things for the benefit of the church (cf. Roose 2005: 139). Later Paul will say that Christ is the head of the church (5:23; cf. Col. 1:18) and that Christians should “grow up to him in every respect, who is the head” (Eph. 4:15; cf. Col. 2:19).[16] Here his point is different: he wants to emphasize that Christ is the head over all the inimical forces of the universe and that he serves in this capacity for the benefit of the church (cf. Col. 2:10).

1:23 Paul now adds a thought in two parts, which describes the church in greater detail. The first part is relatively straightforward. The church to which God gave Christ as head over all things is the church ἥτις ἐστὶν τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ (hētis estin to sōma autou, which is, in truth, his body). Although the indefinite relative pronoun is often used simply for the relative pronoun in the NT (BDF §293), Paul shows in Ephesians that he can distinguish between the two (4:19). The ἥτις here, therefore, probably does not merely mean “which” but carries a qualitative force and should be translated “which, in fact” (Abbott 1897: 34) or “which in truth” (Eadie 1883: 107; cf. BDAG 729–30). If this is right, then Paul wants to place special emphasis on his statement that the church is Christ’s body: it is indeed his body.

Prior to Colossians, Paul compares the church to a body in letters to Corinth and Rome as a way of urging Christians in those cities to set aside their divisiveness and seek unity with one another. “Is Christ divided?” Paul asks in 1 Corinthians (1:13). Later he develops at length the notion that the church consists of many members, but that, just as with the human body, all these members belong to the same body and so should work together humbly, not elevating people with a highly desirable gift above others (1 Cor. 12:12–31). In this discussion, Paul assumes that the body of which he speaks is Christ and that all believers have been baptized “into” (εἰς, eis) this “one body” (ἓν σῶμα, hen sōma, 1 Cor. 12:12–13, 27; cf. 10:16–17), but this aspect of the metaphor falls into the background in order to emphasize the need for unity in the divided Corinthian church by comparing it with a body whose members work together harmoniously.[17]

In Romans, Paul makes the same comparison between the human body and the body of believers with its different “members” (μέλη, melē), each gifted by God and each connected to the other. “We who are many,” Paul says, “are one body in Christ” (οἱ πολλοὶ ἓν σῶμά ἐσμεν ἐν Χριστῷ, hoi polloi hen sōma esmen en Christō; Rom. 12:4–6). His use of the metaphor in Romans is less elaborate than his use of it in 1 Corinthians, however, and does not make the explicit statement that Christians, considered together, comprise the body of Christ (cf. 1 Cor. 12:12, 27).

When we move to Colossians, we find Paul developing the metaphor in two new directions. First, the idea that the ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia, church) is the body of Christ rises to prominence. In Colossians the notion that the church is a harmoniously working body is present (3:15; cf. 2:19) but is less prominent than the idea that the church is the body of Christ (1:18, 24).[18] Second, instead of equating his readers simply with the body of Christ, which possesses, for example, a foot, a hand, an eye, an ear, a nose, and a head (1 Cor. 12:15–21), Paul now introduces the more complex notion that Christ is the head of his church-body (Col. 1:18). This body grows (like the human body), and Christ, as its head, is the source of this growth (2:19).

The false teaching that had troubled the Colossian church seems to have prompted this second development (Bruce 1977: 421; O’Brien 1982: 49–50; Murphy-O’Connor 1996: 246). The false teachers placed Christ alongside other spiritual powers and insisted that these other powers needed to be placated with various ascetic rituals (Col. 2:16–19). Against this diminution of Christ’s significance, Paul asserts Christ’s preeminence and uses the “head” metaphor to do this. Christ is the head of the church so that he might have preeminence in all things (1:18), and the false teachers have failed to hold fast to this head (2:19).

In Ephesians, Paul’s use of the metaphor is reminiscent of his use of it in all three of the other letters, but it also receives some further development. In Ephesians, just as in 1 Corinthians and Romans, the church is made up of various members who should work together harmoniously as a “body” (4:4, 11–13, 15–16, 24–25; 5:30), although the figure of a single body with many harmoniously working parts is not as prominent as it is in those earlier letters (Dunn 1992: 149–50; Best 1998: 193). Just as in Colossians, Christ is the head of his church-body, and as the head, he supports his body’s growth (Eph. 4:15–16; 5:23; cf. Col. 1:18; 2:19).

Two new uses of the metaphor, however, emerge in Ephesians. First, in 2:15–16 Paul will describe the unity of Gentile and Jewish Christians through the cross as a union of the two groups in “one body.” He then implies that this “one body” is a new human that replaces the fallen Adam.

Second, as we have just seen in the exegesis of 1:22, Paul in Ephesians uses the head metaphor independently to speak of Christ’s victorious rule over the inimical powers of the cosmos. In this specific capacity as head over all things (particularly the inimical powers), God has given Christ to the church. Here the metaphor takes a direction unique in the Pauline corpus. Christ is the head over all things, and God has given him this role for the benefit of the church. The church, moreover, is the body of this Christ who is head over all things. Christ is not said to be head over all things and therefore head of the church, but head over all things and, since the church is his body, identifiable with the church. The church, then, is also in some sense head over all inimical powers, and they lie conquered beneath its feet, just as they lie conquered beneath Christ’s feet. Paul will make this point more explicitly in 2:6, where he says that his readers have been raised with Christ and seated in the heavenly places “in Christ Jesus” at God’s right hand.[19]

This now helps us to make sense of the difficult expression τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν πληρουμένου (to plērōma tou ta panta en pasin plēroumenou, that which is full of the One who is continuously and completely filled). This statement is difficult because the noun πλήρωμα (plērōma) can be taken actively (“that which makes something full”) or passively (“that which is full of something”; BDAG 829–30), and the participle πληρουμένου (plēroumenou) could be in the middle voice (“the one who fills for himself”), in the active voice but with a middle form (“the one who fills”), or in the passive voice (“the one who is filled”).

Although an ancient reading of the phrase takes it to mean that the church in some sense completes Christ (e.g., Origen [Heine 2002: 116–17]; Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 3; NPNF 13:62; PG 62:26; cf. Calvin 1965: 138), this is probably not what Paul meant. Elsewhere in the letter where the word πλήρωμα or its verbal cognate πληρόω (plēroō, fill) appears in connection with believers, they are filled with God’s fullness (3:19) or in the Spirit (5:18), and by growing, they expand to the size of Christ’s fullness (4:13). Christ fills all things (4:10). In other words, believers play a passive or neutral role (they are filled or grow to match Christ’s fullness), whereas Christ plays an active role (he fills; cf. Schnackenburg 1991: 81; Best 1998: 188). Here, then, Paul probably meant that the church was “that which is full of” something or someone.

What or who fills the church? Again, we should probably understand πληρουμένου in a passive sense. It could be in the active voice despite its middle/passive form (e.g., Moule 1953: 25; BDAG 828; Lincoln 1990: 77; O’Brien 1999: 151), but elsewhere in Ephesians Paul chooses the appropriate form and voice of this verb for what he wishes to say (4:10; 5:18).[20] If we then move to the middle voice (e.g., Winer 1881: 258; Eadie 1883: 114; Robertson 1923: 805–6; Howard 1974: 351–52), we produce the idea that the church is that which is filled by Christ, who fills everything for himself. Such a reading, however, would make the statement stick out from the flow of Paul’s thought like a sore thumb. The passage emphasizes how God’s action through Christ benefits the church, not how Christ’s action benefits himself (cf. Lincoln 1990: 77). The passive voice, therefore, makes the best sense: the church is that which is filled by the One who is himself filled, presumably Christ (e.g., Best 1998: 188; Dawes 1998: 241, 244–45; Hoehner 2002: 298–99).[21] Since the participle is in the present tense, moreover, Paul probably intends his readers to understand this filling as something that takes place continually.

What or who fills Christ? Paul does not say explicitly, and this adds to the ambiguity of the expression. Colossians provides some help, however, since there the fullness of deity dwells continuously in Christ (Col. 2:9; cf. 1:19). The church, therefore, is filled by Christ, and Christ himself is filled by God.[22]

We now need to fit the phrase τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν (ta panta en pasin) into the puzzle, and this too poses some difficulty. Paul uses the phrase twice elsewhere (1 Cor. 12:6; 15:28). In these other occurrences, part of the phrase (τὰ πάντα) serves as the direct object of an active-voice verb, and part of it (ἐν πᾶσιν) modifies that verb adverbially: the same God works “all things [i.e., gifts of service] in everyone” (1 Cor. 12:6), and God will be “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).[23] If we take the participle πληρουμένου as a passive-voice participle, however, then the phrase cannot function in the way it does in these other two passages. As a passive, πληρουμένου cannot take a direct object, and so the entire phrase τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν must modify πληρουμένου adverbially: “the one who is filled entirely.” This use of the phrase would be unusual, but in light of the difficulties involved in taking πληρουμένου as anything but passive, this solution seems to be the best choice. If the phrase is used adverbially, then it probably functions in the same way as the classical expression παντάπασι, an adverb meaning “entirely, wholly, altogether” (LSJ 1299; Moule 1959: 160; Best 1998; cf. BDAG 783).[24]

If we now put all this together, Paul is saying that the church, as Christ’s body, is filled by Christ who is himself continually and completely filled (by God). The thought is close to Paul’s comment in Col. 2:9–10. There Paul tells the Colossians they should not fall under the spell of human fabrications parading as “philosophy”: “. . . because in [Christ] all the fullness [πλήρωμα] of the Deity dwells bodily [σωματικῶς, sōmatikōs], and you have been filled [πεπληρωμένοι, peplērōmenoi] in him, who is the head of all rule and authority [ὅς ἐστιν ἡ κεφαλὴ πάσης ἀρχῆς καὶ ἐξουσίας, hos estin hē kephalē pasēs archēs kai exousias].” Why did Paul express himself in such a difficult way in Ephesians when he could have spelled out his meaning as clearly as he had in Colossians? Alliteration using the p sound was a highly prized rhetorical device in the first and second centuries, and he may have been more concerned with the majestic rhetorical effect that he created with the phrase τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν πληρουμένου (to plērōma tou ta panta en pasin plēroumenou) than with making the phrase easy to understand.[25] The basic point was clear enough: the messianic king, whom God has made victorious over all the cosmic forces ranged against his people, is united with the church, which because of this union is also victorious over these evil forces.

Summary

In 1:20–23 Paul explains more fully what he meant by saying in 1:19 that he prayed for his readers to understand the greatness of the power that God had exercised on behalf of the church. In 1:20–22a he explains more specifically what he means by God’s great power: it is the power that has raised Christ from the dead, seated him victorious at his right hand, and placed all the cosmic enemies of God beneath Christ’s feet. In 1:22b–23 Paul explains more specifically what he means in saying that God used his power for the church. God has given Christ to the church in his role as victor and head over all things, including the enemies of God and his people. Christ and the church, his body, are one; thus Christ’s victory is also the church’s victory.



Additional Note

1:22. A vigorous and sometimes heated debate surrounds the figurative meaning of the term κεφαλή in the NT. The debate was sparked by Paul’s use of the term with respect to the relationship between husbands and wives in 1 Cor. 11:3 and Eph. 5:23. One side argues that in ancient Greek generally, κεφαλή rarely carried connotations of authority or leadership (e.g., B. Mickelsen and A. Mickelsen 1986; Cervin 1989; Perriman 1994). The other side maintains that the term carried these connotations frequently enough that they would not have seemed foreign to first-century Greek speakers (e.g., Grudem 1985; 1991; 2002; Fitzmyer 1989; 1993). Some scholars have argued that κεφαλή could be used metaphorically to refer to the “source” of something rather than its authoritative head. They have then connected this meaning with the use of the creation narrative in the wider contexts of 1 Cor. 11:3 and Eph. 5:23 (1 Cor. 11:8, 12; Eph. 5:31). Although this understanding of the term originated outside the debate over what the NT teaches about the roles of husband and wife in marriage (Bedale 1954; 1956), it was nevertheless drawn into the debate by those who argued that κεφαλή did not carry connotations of authority (e.g., B. Mickelsen and A. Mickelsen 1986: 105–6). A reasonable case can be made that in Eph. 4:15–16 the κεφαλή of the body is the source of its strength (Dawes 1998: 144–47), although it is difficult to escape additional connotations of authority for the term in that passage.

Perriman (1994: 618) believes that the evidence for either “authority” or “source” is unimpressive and that the term basically meant “that which is most prominent, foremost, uppermost, pre-eminent.” He also observes, however, that the critical element in determining the meaning of the metaphor in any particular instance is the literary context of that particular use (1994: 613, 617; cf. Dawes 1998: 127). Here in 1:22 the context emphasizes Christ’s authority over all things as a result of the victory that God has given to him, and so this must count as an example of the use of κεφαλή to communicate the authority of the person who is the head (cf. LXX: Judg. 11:11; 2 Sam. 22:44).





III. Thanksgiving for Conversion and Intercession for Understanding (1:15–23)

IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)

V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)

VI. Paul’s Divinely Given Task and His Suffering for the Gentiles (3:1–13)


IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)

In 2:1–10 Paul shows his readers how the mighty power of God, demonstrated in the resurrection and victorious enthronement of his Messiah, affects them individually. Paul has just said that God gave Christ, in his capacity as victor over the inimical heavenly powers, to the church, and now he wants to make especially clear to his readers that, since they have believed the gospel, they have experienced personally the effects of this victory. It is true (Lincoln 1990: 85) that Paul continues to speak in corporate terms: he describes his readers’ plight in cosmic language and uses plural pronouns. Yet there is a personal character to the passage also.[1] Paul describes his readers as people with cravings, flesh, desires, and thoughts (v. 3). They receive salvation through faith (v. 8), and it comes as a gift lest “anyone” (τις, tis; singular) should boast (v. 9).

The passage shows how, in personal terms, the great power of God, exhibited in the resurrection and enthronement of Christ, took Paul’s readers from existence under the power of the world, the Ruler of the demonic realm, and their own disobedient nature (vv. 1–3) into a position of victory over these forces (vv. 4–7). It describes how they moved from being objects of God’s justified wrath against those who disobey him (v. 3) to products of God’s re-creative handiwork (v. 10), from walking in trespasses and sins (vv. 1–2) to walking in the good works that God created them to do (v. 10). This movement has happened by their union with the living, risen, and enthroned Christ (vv. 5–6). It came to them as an entirely free gift (v. 5), received by faith (vv. 8–9), and as the result of God’s richly merciful and loving character (v. 4).

The passage can be divided into three sections, corresponding to its three leading thoughts. In 2:1–3 Paul describes his readers’ former plight as objects of God’s wrath. In 2:4–7 he describes God’s salvation of his readers from that plight by the application to them of the power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him, victorious over the inimical spiritual powers of the universe, in the heavenly places (cf. 1:19–23). In 2:8–10 he emphasizes the gracious nature of this salvation.

As Lincoln (1990: 85) has perceptively observed, 2:5 is the central statement of the passage. It gathers together its three main themes and its three parts, first summarizing the plight of Paul and his readers in terms of death in trespasses, next introducing the idea of their union with Christ’s new life, and last, anticipating the final discussion of God’s grace.

This logical and balanced conceptual structure, however, is expressed in a syntactically disjointed way, probably betraying the occasional and oral nature of the letter’s origin. Paul apparently began writing the section intending to say something similar to Col. 2:13 (cf. Eph. 2:1 and 2:5–6). Perhaps having formulated the sentence in Colossians fairly recently, he began 2:1 in much the same way but then realized that his desire to stress the abundance of God’s grace to the readers of Ephesians required a more detailed description of their preconversion plight (2:1–3). Finally satisfied with his expression of the plight, he turned to God’s gracious solution to that plight (2:4), summarized the plight again (2:5a) to contrast it vividly with God’s gracious rescue, and then finally completed the sentence (2:5b–7). Before the sentence was complete, however, he interjected the declaration “By grace you are saved” (2:5b) in anticipation of his fuller discussion of God’s grace (2:8–9). Finally, he described the gracious and accomplished nature of salvation and briefly summarized its ethical results in the lives of the saved (2:10).





IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)

A. Children of Wrath Like All the Rest (2:1–3)

B. Objects of God’s Mercy (2:4–7)

C. The Nature and Consequences of God’s Grace (2:8–10)


A. Children of Wrath Like All the Rest (2:1–3)

In 2:1–3 Paul concentrates on what his believing readers “once” (ποτέ) were (vv. 2–3). The passage falls into three parts. In 2:1 Paul uses the second-person address in turning to his readers and applying God’s powerful actions in Christ on behalf of the church (described in 1:19–23) directly to them: “And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and sins. . . .”[1] Before their conversion, Paul tells them, they had lived in rebellion against God, transgressing his law and sinning against him.

In 2:2 Paul, apparently unsatisfied with the brevity of the description of his readers’ preconversion plight in 2:1, begins to digress from his original sentence and digs more deeply into the nature of their plight.[2] He does this in three ways. First, he describes their death in sin as a living death: they walked around in their sins. Second, he says that his readers lived according to the standards of a world in rebellion against God. Third, he claims that the chief of the spiritual powers inimical to God had the letter’s readers under his control.

In 2:3 Paul continues his digression but marks the start of a new thought with a clause whose beginning is similar to the start of 2:2.﻿[3] This new turn both broadens and deepens his description of his readers’ plight. He describes the plight as affecting everyone, not merely his readers. All believers, including Paul, at one time lived in rebellion against God, and all unbelievers, without exception, also live in this way. He also describes the human plight as something that affects the entire person. By birth, human beings possess flesh and thoughts that lead to sinful desires and sinful actions. In sum, he argues that rebellion against God is a state integral to the human condition apart from the gospel: it affects everyone without exception, and it affects everyone profoundly.



Exegesis and Exposition

1And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and sins, 2in which you once walked according to the ⌜Course⌝ of this world, according to the Ruler of the realm of the air, [the Ruler] of ⌜the spirit⌝ now powerfully working within the sons of disobedience; 3among whom we all also once conducted our lives in the cravings of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, just like the rest.

[2:1] Having described how God has made his power effective for all believers (εἰς ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας, eis hēmas tous pisteuontas, for us who believe) by giving Christ the victory over all inimical heavenly powers (1:19–22), Paul again addresses his readers directly (καὶ ὑμᾶς . . . ὑμῶν, kai hymas . . . hymōn, and you . . . your; cf. 1:18) to remind them of how they in particular have benefited from the grace of God (Calvin 1965: 139; Alford 1857: 85; Schnackenburg 1991: 90; Hoehner 2002: 307).[4] Paul begins the new section with an adverbial clause that he will not complete with a main verb (συνεζωοποίησεν, synezōopoiēsen, he made [us] alive together) until 2:5. “You were,” he tells his readers, νεκροὺς τοῖς παραπτώμασιν καὶ ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν (nekrous tois paraptōmasin kai tais hamartiais hymōn, dead in your transgressions and sins). The adjective νεκρός (nekros, dead) was sometimes used metaphorically in Greek literature and philosophy to refer to those who were “morally or spiritually deficient” (BDAG 667; cf. Bultmann, TDNT 4:893). Epictetus (Arrian, Epict. diss. 3.23.28) says, for example, that unless the philosopher makes clear to those who would study with him their ignorant and unhappy state, then both the philosopher and the one to whom he appeals is νεκρός (cf. Luke 15:24, 32). Jesus could use the term to refer to those who did not follow him (Matt. 8:22; Luke 9:60),[5] and he could call the movement from unbelief to belief in him a change from death to life (John 5:24).[6] The early Christian hymn Paul quotes in Eph. 5:14 also used the term this way.

When Paul connects death with sin in Romans, however, he is thinking of death as the biblical penalty for sin, especially sin against the commandment of God (Gen. 2:16–17; 3:3–4; Deut. 30:19; Rom. 1:32; 5:12–14, 18–21; 6:23; 7:9–11; 8:2, 13), and that is probably also the thought here (cf. Col. 2:13).[7] The penalty of death for disobedience could be taken to mean literal, physical death (e.g., Jub. 4.29–30; Sir. 25:24), but Paul was not alone in thinking that it referred also to the general chaos created by sin (e.g., L.A.E. 44) and to separation from God both now and in eternity (e.g., 2 Esd. [4 Ezra] 7:46–61). Before they believed the gospel, Paul’s readers experienced a living death in the vicious way of life they pursued (4:17–19; 5:3–8, 11, 12, 16; cf. Rom. 1:18–32; Col. 1:21). The impending outpouring of God’s eschatological wrath on the final day also hung over their heads like the sword of Damocles (1:14; 5:6; cf. 1 Thess. 1:10; Rom. 2:5–9; Col. 3:6–7).

The double reference to παραπτώματα (paraptōmata, transgressions) and ἁμαρτίαι (hamartiai, sins) may be still another example of the redundancy that is so characteristic of the style of Ephesians (Lincoln 1990: 93; Aletti 2001: 120n21),[8] or it may echo the language of Scripture.[9] In either case, Paul intends to emphasize the sinfulness of his readers’ condition prior to their conversion rather than to make any distinction between “transgressions” and “sins,” as older commentators sometimes thought.[10] When Paul speaks of sin in the undisputed letters, he conceives of it most often in the singular and as a power that holds humanity under its sway and leads them to death. The use of the plural here is sometimes thought to be “wholly unpauline” (Luz 1998: 131; cf. Pokorný 1992: 97; Hübner 1997: 156). This assessment is considerably overstated: Paul can use the plural in his undisputed letters (1 Thess. 2:16; 1 Cor. 15:3; Gal. 1:4; Rom. 4:7; 7:5; 11:27) and even link the resurrection of Christ with rescue from “sins” (ἁμαρτίαι; 1 Cor. 15:17) just as the resurrection of Christ is linked here with rescue from “transgressions” (παραπτώματα; Eph. 2:5).[11]

[2:2] Paul’s readers once “walked” (περιπατέω, peripateō) in their transgressions. This is a characteristically Pauline word for behaving in a particular way and is especially prominent in Colossians (1:10; 2:6; 3:7; 4:5) and Ephesians (2:10; 4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15).[12] In the Pauline corpus, the term is nearly always followed by a prepositional phrase, an adverbial phrase, or a word in the dative case that more closely identifies the mode of living to which the word refers (Seesemann, TDNT 5:944; BDAG 803). Here Paul uses three such phrases.

The phrase ἐν αἷς (en hais, in which) refers back to the transgressions and sins Paul has just mentioned.[13] His readers have walked in them in the sense that, before they believed the gospel, sin dominated their lives (4:17–19; 5:3–8, 11, 12, 16; cf. Col. 1:21; 3:7).

The expression κατὰ τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου (kata ton aiōna tou kosmou toutou, according to the Course of this world) shows that their plight was even deeper than anything their own sin could have produced. As the additional note on αἰών (aiōn) indicates, this term could have a chronological meaning and simply refer to what Paul elsewhere calls “the present evil age” (ὁ αἰὼν ὁ ἐνεστὼς πονηρός, ho aiōn ho enestōs ponēros; Gal. 1:4). This is the way Paul uses the term αἰών in the rest of the letter (1:21; 2:7; 3:9, 11, 21), and his use of the term here is sandwiched between two clearly chronological uses (1:21; 2:7). At about the time that Paul wrote Ephesians, however, αἰών was beginning to take on personal connotations, and Paul’s use of it here seems to participate in that movement. The “αἰών of this world” is not identical with “the Ruler of the realm of the air” in the next κατά phrase, but it is nevertheless something more powerful than simply the period of time that the world lasts in its present condition. It is a powerful mode of existence characterized by rebellion against God (cf. Schlier 1957: 102; Porkorný 1992: 99; Schwindt 2002: 382–83), something like Paul’s personification of sin in Rom. 5:12–8:3.﻿[14] It is the “Course” that a world in rebellion against God takes. Prior to their conversion, Paul’s readers were at its mercy and, as the preposition κατά brings out, lived their lives according to its standards.

The phrase κατὰ τὸν ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος (kata ton archonta tēs exousias tou aeros, according to the Ruler of the realm of the air) takes the plight of Paul’s readers deeper still. The term ἐξουσία (exousia) is sometimes used of the “domain” or “realm” of a king (2 Kings 20:13 LXX; Luke 23:7) and metaphorically of the “realm” that the devil, or Satan, rules (Luke 4:6; cf. 22:53; Acts 26:18; Col. 1:13). The domain of which Paul speaks here is the ἀήρ (aēr, air). In ancient Aristotelian cosmology, the ἀήρ was the region below the moon and above the earth (Urmson 1990: 10), and in much ancient thinking, it was also the habitation of spiritual powers. Plutarch (Mor. 274b), describing an ancient view with which he seems to agree, says that “the open air” (ὁ ὕπαιθρος ἀήρ, ho hypaithros aēr) is “full of gods and demons.”[15] Diogenes Laertius (Vit. phil. 8.32), describing the view of Pythagoras, says that “all the air [ἀέρα, aera] is full of souls [ψυχῶν, psychōn], and these are also called [ὀνομάζεσθαι, onomazesthai] demons [δαίμονας, daimonas] and divinized, departed human beings [ἥρωας, hērōas].”[16] These powers were thought to send people dreams and visions. They needed to be placated and wooed with “purifications and lustrations . . . divination, and the like” (Vit. phil. 8.32).[17] They were also the object of magical incantations that sought to control them. Clearly, the powers that inhabited the air were widely feared.[18]

For Paul, the “air” was probably part of the “heavenly places” and the location, within them, of “every name that is named” (πᾶς ὄνομα ὀνομαζόμενος, pas onoma onomazomenos, 1:21). These names signified the inimical spiritual powers over whom God had given Christ the victory when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand (1:20–21; cf. 6:12). Christ’s place in the heavens is high above them (1:21; 4:10), and they are beneath his feet (1:22). Before they believed the gospel, Paul’s readers lived according to the norms of the Ruler of these evil beings, and in Ephesians, this Ruler could only be “the devil” (4:27; 6:11–12).[19]

The devil is not only the ruler of the air but is also the ruler τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ νῦν ἐνεργοῦντος ἐν τοῖς υἱοῖς τῆς ἀπειθείας (tou pneumatos tou nyn energountos en tois hyiois tēs apeitheias, of the spirit now at work within the sons of disobedience). As the additional note on τοῦ πνεύματος explains, this term probably refers to the evil, spiritual force that is at work within οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς ἀπειθείας (hoi hyioi tēs apeitheias, the sons of disobedience; cf. 1 Cor. 2:12). The word ἀπείθεια (apeitheia) carries the connotation not merely of disobedience to a command but also of unbelief, a heartfelt refusal to place one’s confidence in something (BDAG 99; cf. 4 Macc. 8:7–9; Rom. 11:30). In Ephesians, therefore, “the sons of disobedience” are those who have not believed “the word of truth, the gospel of . . . salvation” (1:13) and who, because of this, stand under the wrath of God (5:6; cf. 1:14; 2:3).[20] A spiritual force is powerfully at work (ἐνεργοῦντος, energountos, working) in these people, and the Ruler of the realm of the air, in which God’s spiritual enemies are active, also presides over this spiritual force, which influences the behavior of those in rebellion against God.

In summary, before Paul’s readers heard and believed the gospel, they were walking in their own transgressions of God’s law. They also walked according to the standard set by the world around them and according to the norms of the one who rules both the demonic realm and the spiritual force that powerfully pervades that realm.

[2:3] Paul now emphasizes that this plight affected every human being, including himself (ἐν οἷς καὶ ἡμεῖς πάντες ἀνεστράφημέν ποτε, en hois kai hēmeis pantes anestraphēmen pote, among whom we all also once conducted our lives). A vast company of interpreters has argued that the phrase καὶ ἡμεῖς (kai hēmeis, we also) means “we Jews also,” and that Paul now broadens his description of his Gentile readers’ plight to include in it all humanity, even the Jewish people.[21] Paul certainly does this in Romans (2:17; 3:19, 22b–23), but in Ephesians ethnicity does not enter the argument until 2:11.﻿[22] Here in 2:3, those who first heard this letter read would have no way of knowing that the first-person plural meant anything other than what it meant when it last appeared in the text. There it had clearly referred to Paul and his readers (ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας, hēmas tous pisteuontas, “us who believe,” 1:19), not to Paul and his fellow Jews. Here, then, Paul shifts to the first-person plural and repeats the substance of 2:2a (ἐν αἷς ποτε περιεπατήσατε, en hais pote periepatēsate, in which you once walked) in order to show that the plight he has just described has affected every Christian, without exception, himself included. It is not as if his readers lived especially evil lives before they believed the gospel: every human being was numbered among “the sons of disobedience” of verses 1 and 2.﻿[23] It is a plight, therefore, that all believers, no matter who they are, once shared with “the rest” (οἱ λοιποί, hoi loipoi) of unbelieving humanity.

In this verse Paul also extends his description of the plight his readers and all Christians suffered before they believed the gospel. He does this in two ways. First, he says that the human plight covered the entire person: mind and flesh, thoughts and deeds. Before they believed the gospel, Paul and his readers lived in the “cravings” (ἐπιθυμίαις, epithymiais) of their flesh, performing the “desires” (θελήματα, thelēmata) of the flesh. They also performed the desires of their “thoughts” (διανοιῶν, dianoiōn).

Paul can occasionally use the term ἐπιθυμία (epithymia) to refer to a “desire” for something good (Phil. 1:23; 1 Thess. 2:17), but most of the time he uses it in a negative way.[24] In Galatians and Romans, he connects ἐπιθυμία closely with “flesh” (σάρξ, sarx), and he draws a contrast between Christian existence and behavior on one hand and the cravings of the “flesh” on the other (Gal. 5:16, 24; Rom. 13:14). In its only other use in Ephesians (4:22), Paul connects it, as he does here, with the old “manner of life” (ἀναστροφή, anastrophē) that his readers were taught to abandon when they heard and believed the gospel. There he adds that ἐπιθυμίαι (epithymiai, cravings) are “deceitful” (τῆς ἀπάτης, tēs apatēs) and connects them with the “continual corruption” (φθειρόμενον, phtheiromenon) of humanity. Here, then, “the cravings of our flesh” are the deceitful, evil desires that arise from the human tendency toward rebellion against God and subsequent self-destruction.

The term θέλημα (thelēma, desire), at least in the Pauline corpus, is a more neutral word than ἐπιθυμία. God (1:9; 6:6; cf. 1 Thess. 4:3; Rom. 2:18; 12:2; Col. 1:9; 4:12), Christ (5:17; cf. 1 Thess. 5:18), the devil (2 Tim. 2:26), and people generally (1 Cor. 16:12) all will or desire that certain events happen (BDAG 447). Here, however, the term’s link to both ἐπιθυμία and σάρξ gives it a clearly negative connotation. Since θέλημα appears in 1 Cor. 7:37 with the meaning “sexual desire” (cf. John 1:13), and since in Eph. 5:3–6 Paul expresses concern that his readers not lapse into the inappropriate sexual conduct of “the sons of disobedience” (cf. 2:2), it is possible that the term also carries a hint of that meaning here (Schrenk, TDNT 3:61). Here it makes a rare appearance in the plural, a form in which it can refer to sexual desires in the magical papyri.[25]

The term διάνοιαι (dianoiai, thoughts) describes the result of mental processes or reflections (Behm, TDNT 4:963–64). “The converse of the soul with itself, without speech, is what we called thought [διάνοια],” says Plato (Soph. 263e, quoted from Urmson 1990: 41). It is not normally a negative part of the human psychological makeup, but in this context it clearly has negative connotations of mental decisions that run counter to what God desires (cf. 4:18; Num. 15:39 LXX; Sir. 29:16; 2 Macc. 2:2; 1 Esd. 4:26). Paul elsewhere calls this “the mind of the flesh” (τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός, to phronēma tēs sarkos), which is “at enmity with God” (ἔχθρα εἰς θεόν, echthra eis theon), is unable to submit to his law (Rom. 8:5, 7; cf. Rom. 1:21, 28; Col. 2:18), and needs to be renewed (Rom. 12:2).[26]

The cravings and desires of the flesh and the desires of the thoughts gave way, Paul says, to actions (ἀνεστράφημεν . . . ποιοῦντες, anestraphēmen . . . poiountes, we lived . . . doing). The whole package—flesh and mind, deeds and thoughts—placed everyone squarely among the “sons of disobedience” (cf. 4:17–19).

Paul’s description of the flesh as “ours” (ἡμῶν, hēmōn) and his use of the basically neutral terms θέλημα and διάνοια in this passage show that he thinks of neither the flesh nor the mind as outside powers that have driven people, against their will, into rebellion against God.[27] All humankind has chosen willfully and thoughtfully to live among the sons of disobedience and to act on their rebellious cravings, desires, and thoughts.

This is not the whole story, however; so Paul adds a second element to his description of the human plight in verses 1–2. All (including himself) are τέκνα φύσει ὀργῆς (tekna physei orgēs, children of wrath by nature). Ὀργῆς (orgēs, of wrath) is a “genitive of destination,” describing the destiny of the children (cf. Rom. 9:22).[28] Before Paul and his readers embraced the gospel of salvation (1:13), they were destined for the eschatological outpouring of God’s wrath upon the disobedient (cf. Matt. 3:7; Luke 3:7; 1 Thess. 1:10; 5:9; Rom. 2:5, 8; 3:5; 5:9; 12:19; Col. 3:6), a process that Paul believed had already begun (Rom. 1:18; Eph. 5:6).

This destiny, moreover, was theirs φύσει (physei, by nature). This term referred to the condition into which someone was born, and the dative singular of the word, the form Paul uses here, often meant “by birth.”[29] Paul uses the term here, therefore, to emphasize that although unbelieving human beings are culpable for their sinful cravings, desires, and thoughts (vv. 1–3a), they have chosen this path inevitably, in agreement with the state into which they were born (cf. Rom. 5:12; 2 Esd. [4 Ezra] 7:62–69, 116–18).[30]

Summary

In 2:1–3 Paul begins to describe how God’s great power has benefited individuals within the church by emphasizing the depth of the sinful plight in which everyone was mired. This plight was all-encompassing. Everyone, without exception, chose to sin. They received encouragement to do this by the norms laid down within the rebellious system of this world and by the invisible Ruler of the cosmic realm of evil. They also received encouragement to sin by their own tendency to rebel against God, a tendency that came naturally to them and was expressed in the outworking of their thoughts and desires. In a way reminiscent of Rom. 1:18–3:20, Paul has described the plight of human rebellion against God in the bleakest terms. There are no exceptions to it and, humanly speaking, no escape from it. Just as in Rom. 3:21–26, then, the description of the grace of God in 2:4–10 comes as an immense relief.



Additional Notes

2:2. The meaning of the term αἰών in 2:2 is not entirely clear. It can mean “a segment of time as a particular unit of history, age” (BDAG 32). This meaning is common in other writers of Paul’s period, whether Christian, Jewish, or pagan, and Paul often uses the term this way.[31] Paul has already used it with this temporal sense in 1:21 and seems to use it again this way in 2:7, so the decision to read the term as “age” in 2:2 at first seems obvious (Lincoln 1990: 94–95; O’Brien 1999: 158–59; Hoehner 2002: 310). Since αἰών can have a spatial meaning (“world”) as well as a temporal meaning (“age”), the qualifying reference to the κόσμος would simply be another example of Paul’s (or the author’s) redundant style in this letter (Masson 1953: 158n3; Lincoln 1990: 95; Muddiman 2001: 103).[32] This reading of the phrase is reasonable and may well be correct.

The redundant style of Ephesians, however, might also support reading αἰών here as the name of an invisible being. Paul’s next words comprise another prepositional phrase, headed by κατά, that describes the former lives of his Christian readers as lived “according to” a being that Paul says is a “ruler.” This invisible power is probably identical with “the devil,” which Paul mentions later in the letter (4:27; 6:11). If this κατά phrase stands parallel to the first κατά phrase, then it describes again the object of that phrase and does so in unmistakably personal terms. The resulting translation of both phrases would then be “according to the Aeon of this world, according to the Ruler of the realm of the air. . . .” The terms “aeon” and “ruler” would refer to the same inimical spiritual power.

The theory that a god called αἰών was worshiped as early as 200 BC in Egypt (e.g., Reitzenstein 1921: 188–207; Sasse, TDNT 1:198; Bruce 1984: 282; Lincoln 1990: 94; cf. Barth 1974: 214; Muddiman 2001: 103) is based on evidence of uncertain historical worth (Epiphanius, Pan. 51.22.8–10; Historia Alexandri Magni 30.6) and is probably not correct (Nock 1934: 92–97; Fraser 1972: 336–37; Drijvers, DDD 13–14).[33] At least by the early second century AD, however, the term was used to refer to deity, if not to a particular deity with its own cult. Epictetus (Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.5.13) can say, “I am not αἰών but a human being, a part of everything as an hour is a part of a day.” Does he mean that he is not “eternal”?[34] If so, it seems odd that he used the noun αἰών rather than the adjective αἰώνιος. Still, he uses the term later in a clearly temporal sense to refer to a statue that does not move “for the whole αἰών” (Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.8.20).

A similar ambiguity occurs at about the same time in Ignatius. He uses the term primarily in a temporal sense (Eph. inscr.; 8.1; 17.1; 19.1; Magn. 1.2; 6.1; Trall. 4.2; Rom. 6.1; 7.1; Phld. 6.2; Smyrn. 1.2), but in Eph. 19.2, just after speaking of “the ruler of this age” he asks, “How then was he [Christ] manifested to the aeons”?[35] This could be a temporal reference, but it makes somewhat better sense as a reference to inimical spiritual powers, Aeons. By the second century, “the name Aion was in the air” (Nock 1934: 97): it began to appear on coins in connection with the Roman emperor, it cropped up as a deity or class of deities, especially within gnosticism (e.g., Irenaeus, Haer. 1.1.1; 1.30.2, 11; Hippolytus, Haer. 6.14.6; PGL 56), and it appeared in the magical papyri (Nock 1934: 78, 83–84; Arnold 1989: 59). Evidence such as this has led a number of commentators to see Paul’s use of αἰών in 2:2 as a reference to an evil personal power—“the god of this age” (ὁ θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου), as he calls him in 2 Cor. 4:4, or “the devil,” as he will call him in Eph. 4:27 and 6:11 (e.g., Gnilka 1971: 114; Schnackenburg 1991: 91; Best 1998; BDAG 33).[36]

Against this interpretation, it is commonly said that Paul always uses the term αἰών elsewhere in its temporal sense and has done so in the immediate context of 2:2 (cf. 1:21; 2:7). To suddenly use it here of a personal power, the argument goes, would be confusing (Arnold 1989: 59; O’Brien 1999: 158–59; cf. MacDonald 2000: 229; Hoehner 2002: 310). As we have just seen, however, this is exactly the state of affairs with Ignatius, and something similar happens with Epictetus. Every use of the term in Ignatius is temporal, except Eph. 19.2, and that one use occurs directly after a temporal use of the term. Epictetus uses the term only twice in his extant corpus, but here too a use that seems to mean “god” (Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.5.13) is followed by a clearly temporal use (2.8.20).

In light of the ambiguous evidence, a firm decision on the meaning of αἰών in 2:2 does not seem possible. It is probably best to conclude, with the author of one of the most thorough discussions of the issue (Schwindt 2002: 379–83), that already in the undisputed writings of Paul the terms αἰών and κόσμος overlap, just as they do here, to describe less a chronological concept than a powerful sphere of existence that is opposed to God (1 Cor. 1:20; 2:6; 3:18). In the second half of the first century and the first half of the second century, the term was beginning to gather around it the connotations of personal power that would eventually become explicit in the second half of the second century.

2:2. The genitive phrase τοῦ πνεύματος is ambiguous and has been understood in a number of different ways. It could stand in apposition to τὸν ἄρχοντα, with the result that the ruler is renamed as “the spirit now at work among the sons of disobedience” (Masson 1953: 158; Gnilka 1971: 115n4; cf. Robinson 1904: 154–55). Since nouns in apposition to each other normally occupy the same case, and since τὸν ἄρχοντα is accusative whereas τοῦ πνεύματος is genitive, it is necessary, on this explanation, to believe that the genitive-case words immediately before and after τοῦ πνεύματος have driven it into the genitive case.

If this seems implausible, and we choose to follow normal Greek grammar and syntax exactly, τοῦ πνεύματος would stand in apposition to the genitive case noun that immediately precedes it, τοῦ ἀέρος. Τοῦ πνεύματος would then mean that the evil “atmosphere” over which the devil rules is a spiritual atmosphere of resistance to the gospel (Schlier 1957: 104–5). In this passage, however, ἀήρ seems to be the geographical location of the ruler’s realm. It is the place where evil spiritual beings dwell, not the evil atmosphere that they produce (cf. Haupt 1902a: 51).

Perhaps, then, τοῦ πνεύματος is closely related to τῆς ἐξουσίας and refers to the evil spirits that exist in the devil’s realm, conceived as a single group at work in those who are rebellious against God (Alford 1857: 87; Eadie 1883: 129; E. Scott 1930: 163). Here again, however, grammar stands in the way: if Paul intended to speak of evil “spirits,” why did he use the singular?

Probably we should take τοῦ πνεύματος as syntactically parallel to τῆς ἐξουσίας and dependent, like τῆς ἐξουσίας, on τὸν ἄρχοντα. Τοῦ πνεύματος might then point backward to τῆς ἐξουσίας and refer to the evil “spirit” that pervades the devil’s realm, that the devil presides over as ruler, and that is also at work in those who are disobedient to God (Ellicott 1859: 34; Abbott 1897: 42; Haupt 1902a: 51–52; Lincoln 1990: 97). Alternatively, τοῦ πνεύματος might point forward to τοῖς υἱοῖς τῆς ἀπειθείας and refer to the interior life of those who rebel against God: the ruler not only presides over the realm of the air but also over the spiritual aspect of people who are disobedient to God (Hoehner 2002: 315; Wallace 1996: 103). Paul can use the term “spirit” in Ephesians of the spiritual faculty within human beings (4:23), and this may be the way he is using it here. On balance, however, it seems more likely that Paul would speak of an evil force “working” (ἐνεργοῦντος) within the disobedient than of the inward, spiritual part of the disobedient being at work in them. If we see “spirit” here as a reference to an evil force, then it forms an antithetical parallel to God himself, who “effected” (ἐνήργησεν) the resurrection and exaltation of Christ (1:20; cf. 2 Cor. 4:12) and in doing this defeated the inimical powers that populate the devil’s realm (Eph. 1:21–22).





IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)

A. Children of Wrath Like All the Rest (2:1–3)

B. Objects of God’s Mercy (2:4–7)

C. The Nature and Consequences of God’s Grace (2:8–10)


B. Objects of God’s Mercy (2:4–7)

Paul now offers the positive counterpart to the dark shadows of the human plight described in 2:1–3. Although sin, encouraged by human rebellion, evil spiritual forces, the flesh, and the mind, had made Paul and his readers objects of God’s justified wrath (2:1–3), God has responded to their situation by uniting them to the risen and victorious Christ (2:5–6).

In 2:4–7 Paul wants to emphasize two elements of this response. First, he wants his readers to understand that God’s response has arisen from his persistently merciful, loving, and gracious character. Paul communicates this in both explicit and subtle ways. He speaks in explicitly effusive language of God’s “rich” mercy, his “great” love, and the “surpassing wealth” of his grace. He also clearly attributes the motive for God’s saving work on behalf of believers to God’s character. He has rescued them “because” of his mercy and “on account of” his great love (v. 4) and to “show” them his abundant grace for eternity (v. 7).

On a more subtle level, Paul repeats the substance of the desperate plight he has just described in 2:1–3 immediately before speaking of God’s saving action (2:5a). He seems to do this, in part, to place the depths of the plight and the lavishness of God’s response in striking contrast to each other. In his repetition, moreover, he brings the expression “when you/we were” forward (cf. 2:1, 3; Col. 2:13) to place special emphasis on the timing of God’s mercy: God has rescued believers precisely when they could do nothing to help themselves (cf. Rom. 5:6, 8, 10). When Paul breaks into his own discourse in 2:5b, therefore, with the statement that “by grace you are saved,” it is not surprising that the term “grace” appears first in the phrase. This is where Paul wants the emphasis to lie.

Second, Paul focuses on the critical role of Christ in God’s saving work on his readers’ behalf. He draws a studied parallel between, on the one hand, God’s use of “the might of his strength” to raise Christ from the dead and seat him, victorious over his cosmic enemies, at God’s right hand in heavenly places in 1:19–21 and, on the other hand, his rescue of believers by making them alive together with Christ and raising and seating them together with him in heavenly places. This implies that just as Christ became victorious over death and over the inimical spiritual forces ranged against him (1:21–22a; cf. 6:12), so believers have become victorious over their spiritual death and over “the Ruler of the realm of the air, [the Ruler] of the spirit now powerfully working within the sons of disobedience” (vv. 1–2). This does not mean that believers have become victorious in the same way Christ has—Paul is careful not to say that believers have been exalted to God’s right hand (cf. 2:6 with 1:20)—but the victory that God has given to Christ he has also graciously given to believers because they are “in Christ Jesus” (v. 6) and are therefore united “with” him in his victory over the enemies of God’s people.



Exegesis and Exposition

4But God, because he is rich in mercy, on account of his great love with which he loved us, 5even when we were dead in transgressions, made us alive together ⌜with Christ⌝—⌜by grace⌝ you are saved— 6and raised us together with him and seated us together with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus 7in order that he might show in the coming ages the surpassing wealth of his grace by kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.

[2:4] With the phrase ὁ δὲ θεός (ho de theos, but God), Paul now begins to describe God’s response to the seemingly hopeless plight into which sin, the flesh, the mind, and the demonic world have plunged humanity (2:1–3). Although Paul and his readers deserve God’s wrath (v. 3), God has made it possible for them to escape this otherwise inevitable destiny and to share Christ’s victory over evil (vv. 5–6). Paul begins by announcing the primary theme of the section, a theme that he will pick up again at its conclusion (v. 7): God did this because of his overwhelmingly merciful and loving character. The participle ὤν (ōn, because he is) stands parallel to the causal prepositional phrase διὰ τὴν πολλὴν ἀγάπην αὐτοῦ (dia tēn pollēn agapēn autou, because of his great love) and, like it, indicates the cause of the action described in the sentence’s three main verbs (συνεζωοποίησεν . . . συνήγειρεν . . . συνεκάθισεν, synezōopoiēsen . . . synēgeiren . . . synekathisen). God united Paul and his readers with Christ in his new life, resurrection, and exaltation to God’s right hand because of something about his character: he is rich in mercy and possesses much love.

In emphasizing the abundance of God’s mercy and love, and his willingness, out of this mercy, to rescue his people when they deserve his wrath, Paul is echoing themes familiar from OT, early Jewish, and early Christian contexts. The OT frequently describes the Lord as “abounding in steadfast love” (רַב־חֶסֶד, rab-ḥesed), a phrase that the LXX persistently renders with the single word πολυέλεος (polyeleos, very merciful).[1] In most of the passages where this phrase occurs, God is said to be abundantly merciful precisely within a context where he might justifiably pour out his wrath upon his people or, in the case of its occurrence in Jon. 4:2, on the people of Nineveh (exceptions are Exod. 34:6; Pss. 86:5, 15; 145:8). The phrase is so common in the OT that it was probably used in Jewish liturgy prior to the Second Temple period and has remained in liturgical use in the synagogue in the form of the so-called Thirteen Attributes of God (Exod. 34:6–7) down to the present (Sarna 1991: 216). The concept, if not the precise language, also shows up in Jesus’s parable of the unjust slave, where the king, who represents God, speaks of how he “had mercy” (ἠλέησα, ēleēsa) on a slave who owed him the unimaginable sum of 10,000 talents (Matt. 18:33).

Paul follows his description of God’s rich mercy with a reference to ἡ πολλὴ ἀγάπη αὐτοῦ (hē pollē agapē autou, his great love). Love is an important theme in Ephesians: Paul speaks of God the Father’s love for Christ Jesus (1:6), of God’s love for believers (here in 2:4),[2] of Christ’s love for believers (3:17, 19; 5:1–2, 25), of the love of God and of Christ as the basis for the love that believers should have for one another (5:2, 25, 28; cf. 1:4, 15; 4:2, 15–16; 6:23), and of the love of believers for the Lord Jesus Christ (6:24). The language of love here in 2:4 is intended to reexpress the idea of God’s mercy, and so we should not distinguish between the two concepts, but Paul’s use of ἀγάπη (agapē) and ἀγαπάω (agapaō) to explain God’s mercy, and the emphasis he places on the concept of love through the cognate accusative construction (τὴν . . . ἀγάπην . . . ἣν ἠγάπησεν, tēn . . . agapēn . . . hēn ēgapēsen, the love with which he loved),[3] show the concept’s importance and prepare the way for the prominent place of love in chapters 3–6.

[2:5–6] Before getting to the set of three main verbs on which everything in 2:1–5a depends grammatically, Paul repeats the substance of 2:1.﻿[4] This not only recalls the train of thought that Paul interrupted in 2:2–3 but also throws the bleakness of the human plight and the lavishness of God’s mercy and love into dramatic juxtaposition. Paul makes this juxtaposition especially prominent by bringing the ὄντας (ontas) forward and so emphasizing that it was precisely “when we were” dead that God intervened (cf. Rom. 5:6, 8, 10).[5]

Paul then describes God’s gracious response to the human plight and, in doing so, finally provides the main verbs that govern the opening participial phrase in 2:1. Rescue from the plight described in 2:1–3 and 5a comes through the union of believers with Christ’s new life, his resurrection, and his exaltation to God’s right hand. Just as God used “the might of his strength” to raise Christ from the dead and seat him at his right hand “in the heavenly places” (1:19–20), so he has already raised and seated Christians together with him “in the heavenly places” (Allen 1986: 103–4). Paul uses three verbs that begin with the prepositional prefix σύν (syn) to communicate this, and although in their compounded form the verbs are unusual, the ideas conveyed by the compounded forms are not uncommon in the New Testament.

The first verb, συζωοποιέω (syzōopoieō, make alive together with), appears only here and in the closely related Col. 2:13 in all known Greek literature prior to the Pauline Letters.[6] The Paul of the undisputed letters, however, is fond of verbs compounded with the preposition σύν (e.g., 1 Cor. 4:8; 12:26; Gal. 2:19; Phil. 3:10; 2 Cor. 7:3; Rom. 6:4, 6, 8; 8:17), and uses the verb ζωοποιέω to speak of the link between Christ’s resurrection and the resurrection of believers (Rom. 8:11; cf. 1 Cor. 15:22; Best 1998: 214). He can also use the preposition σύν with the verb ζάω (zaō, live) either separately (1 Thess. 5:10) or in a compounded form (Rom. 6:8), to speak of Christians living with the resurrected Christ. The second σύν verb, συνεγείρω (synegeirō, raise together with), appears only here and in Colossians (2:12; 3:1) in the NT; yet again, the idea that the believer’s resurrection from the dead is closely linked to Christ’s resurrection is common coinage in early Christian literature and is especially characteristic of Paul (1 Cor. 15:12–22, 48). The third term, συγκαθίζω (synkathizō, sit together with), appears only here in a transitive sense in the NT (cf. Luke 22:55), but the thought that the people of God will reign with God or Christ in heaven is not uncommon in literature from the period (Aune 1997: 261–62).[7] The most unusual element about all three verbs is their past tense: here the Christian’s life, resurrection, and royal position with Christ are events that have already happened.[8]

Between the first verb (συνεζωοποίησεν) with its object (τῷ Χριστῷ, tō Christō, with Christ) and the other two verbs, Paul breaks into the sentence with a direct second-person address to his readers that both summarizes what he is trying to say and anticipates the theme of his next paragraph (χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι, chariti este sesōsmenoi, by grace you are saved). Χάρις (charis, grace) recalls the rich mercy and great love of God that Paul has already described in 2:4 and carries these concepts further by emphasizing the absolutely free nature of God’s action on behalf of believers: he acted out of no obligation whatsoever, but only out of his own generosity (cf. 2:7–8; Rom. 3:24; 11:6; Titus 3:7; BDAG 1079). As we have just seen (in the comments on 2:4), the language of God’s abundant mercy and graciousness appears frequently in the OT and Second Temple Judaism. The language specifically of χάρις also surrounded people who lived in the urban areas of the Roman Empire in the first century as a common term used in inscriptions to describe the massively generous benefactions of the Julio-Claudian emperors (Harrison 1999: 83–90; 2003: 48–49).[9] Paul and his readers would have been familiar with this language, and Paul may have intended his audience to see in his own use of it here the implicit claim that in Christ, God’s benefaction toward his people has outstripped anything Rome had to offer (Whitlark 2003).[10]

The phrase ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι is a perfect periphrastic construction that, in this context, describes a present state of being: Paul’s readers are saved.[11] The term σῴζω (sōzō) often refers to rescue from destruction (1 Cor. 1:18; 3:15; 2 Cor. 2:15; Rom. 9:27; Mark 8:35; BDAG 982–83) and is therefore a particularly apt word to use for God’s merciful, gracious, and loving deliverance of believers from the desperate situation Paul has described in 2:1–3.

When Paul speaks of salvation in the undisputed letters, he normally refers to it as something believers will experience in the future, presumably at the final day (1 Thess. 2:16; 1 Cor. 3:15; 5:5; 10:33; Rom. 5:9–10; 9:27; 10:9; 11:26), although he can also describe it as an ongoing event in the present (1 Cor. 1:18; 15:2; 2 Cor. 2:15) and say, “Now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2; cf. Isa. 49:8; Best 1998: 602). In one passage he uses the verb in the aorist tense (ἐσώθημεν, esōthēmen, we were saved) but in a context that emphasizes the future orientation of salvation (Rom. 8:24). In passages where he speaks of persuading others of the truth of the gospel as “saving” them, it is unclear whether salvation is something that happens in the present when the person believes the gospel or in the future (1 Cor. 1:21; 7:16; 9:22; Rom. 11:14).

This evidence means that, like Paul’s use of the aorist tense for the resurrection of believers and their seating with Christ, the use of the perfect tense in Eph. 2:5 and 8 for salvation is unusual. Here salvation is something that is emphatically present for believers.[12] They have already been made alive with Christ, already raised with him, and even already seated with him in heavenly places.[13] Their resurrection has, in some sense, already taken place (cf. Col. 3:1).

Moreover, there is no mention of Christ’s cross here, but only of his resurrection and victorious exaltation, something that stands out all the more when we compare the passage to Rom. 5:6–11 and Col. 2:11–15, passages whose language Eph. 2:5–6 seems to echo. In Rom. 5 Paul describes the plight of people before they embrace the gospel, just as he does in Eph. 2:1 and 5a, by using a form of ὤν (ōn, being) adverbially to emphasize that it was precisely while they were in the grip of weakness (Rom. 5:6), sin (5:8), and hostility to God (5:10) that God rescued them. The rescue of sinners comes not through Christ’s resurrection, however, but through his death (5:6, 8–9a, 10a), and although justification lies in the past (5:1), final salvation is still future (5:9).

In Colossians the rescue comes in part through the union of believers with Christ’s resurrection, but believers are also united, through baptism with Christ’s burial (2:12), and the crucifixion of Christ plays a large role in the triumph of believers over the powers (2:14–15).[14] Rather than depicting believers as already reigning with Christ, moreover, in Colossians the life of believers is hidden with Christ, who sits at God’s right hand, only to be revealed when Christ himself is revealed in the future (3:1–3; cf. 2 Cor. 13:4).
