Is all this a sign that Ephesians comes from a time in which Paul’s apocalyptic outlook (with its expectation of the resurrection and future salvation) has faded and now salvation is accomplished, albeit still by God’s grace, through baptism into the church (Luz 1976: 369–75)? Does this passage show a decided retreat from the Pauline, and even Colossian, teaching on suffering with Christ, a retreat driven by the author’s concern to see baptism as the union between the believer and Christ in his role as “head” (Hahn 2002: 363–64; cf. Berger 1995: 568–69)?

If we have already decided that Ephesians is a pseudonymous production of second-generation Christianity, then we can plausibly answer yes to these questions. There is a striking difference between Ephesians and the seven undisputed Pauline letters in the emphasis placed on dying with, or suffering with, Christ.[15] That difference fits neatly into a particular construal of the history of early Christianity that sees the post-Pauline period as a time when, even among Paulinists, the cross, the Spirit, and apocalyptic elements faded from view and were replaced with ecclesiological and christological emphases.

If Ephesians is Paul’s own, however, then we need imagine nothing more than a shift of emphasis in this particular letter in order to address a particular pastoral situation. Ephesians’ lack of emphasis on suffering with Christ is certainly unusual in light of the prominence of this element in the undisputed letters. If Paul were addressing Christians who were tempted for various reasons to fear the rulers and authorities in heavenly places and to placate them with worship, however, then it is reasonably easy to see why he might express himself this way (cf. Arnold 1989: 147–50, 171). He has prayed that God would enlighten the eyes of his readers to the great power that God has placed at their disposal in raising Christ from the dead and seating him in the heavenly places, victorious over the inimical spiritual powers of the cosmos (1:17–23), and now he shows precisely how God has done this: he did it through their conversion. When they heard and believed the gospel (1:13–14), Christ’s victory over the evil powers became their victory also, for they were released from captivity to the Ruler of the realm of the air (2:2; Arnold 1989: 148). God brought them to life, resurrected them, and seated them with the victorious Christ in heavenly places.

In addition, we should keep in mind that, on one hand, Ephesians is not entirely devoid of the theme of suffering with Christ, and on the other hand, in places the undisputed letters come close to identifying the life of the believer with the resurrected life of Christ. In Ephesians, Paul is a “prisoner of Christ Jesus” (3:1), an “enchained ambassador” (6:20), and his suffering for his readers, he says, leads to their glory (3:13). The substance underlying these statements, while not as dramatically phrased, is identical to 2 Cor. 2:14 (“But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumphal procession [i.e., as a prisoner] in Christ”) and 2 Cor. 4:12 (“Death is at work in us, but life in you”). In 2 Corinthians, Paul says not merely that he carries around the death of Jesus in his body but that he does this so that “the life of Jesus might be visible in our body” (2 Cor. 4:10; cf. 1 Cor. 4:18–21; 2 Cor. 13:3–4).[16] In Romans he says not only that “the body” of believers “is dead because of sin” but also that “the Spirit is life because of righteousness” (Rom. 8:10; cf. 6:4, 13).[17] In Philippians he can say that the “citizenship” of believers “is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).[18] Although he never speaks elsewhere of the enthronement of Christians with Christ, he can speak of Christ living in Christians (Gal. 2:20) and of Christians sharing the heavenly glory of Christ (2 Cor. 3:18; Rom. 8:30; Hübner 1997: 161–62). None of this means that Ephesians and the undisputed letters have the same balance between realized and future eschatological expressions: Ephesians clearly emphasizes the realized aspect of the tension. Nevertheless, what we find in Ephesians does not stand in contradiction to the theology of the undisputed letters but places emphasis on one side of the typical Pauline eschatology because of the situation that the letter addresses.[19]

[2:7] Paul now describes the reason why God has joined believers to Christ’s new life, resurrection, and exaltation. He did this so that for all eternity he might show them, in Christ Jesus and by his kindness, the wealth of his grace. Paul has already spoken of how the costly redemption of believers through the death of Christ demonstrated the abundance of God’s grace (1:7). He has also said that God considers his people to be his abundantly glorious inheritance (1:18) and that God’s purpose for his people is to provide them with an inheritance (1:11; cf. 1:14; Col. 1:12). Now Paul draws these threads together. The phrase ἵνα ἐνδείξηται (hina endeixētai, in order that he might show) indicates the purpose of all four preceding verbs (συνεζωοποίησεν, ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι, συνήγειρεν, and συνεκάθισεν), and the term ἐνδείκνυμι (endeiknymi), a favorite of Paul’s, most often refers to something people reveal about themselves.[20] Sometimes, however, it refers to God’s own demonstration of his character (Rom. 9:17, 22; cf. 1 Tim. 1:16; Rom. 3:25–26), and this is how Paul uses it here.

God saved Paul and his readers for the purpose of demonstrating not merely his grace but “the surpassing [ὑπερβάλλον, hyperballon] wealth of his grace” (cf. 2 Cor. 9:14). For those who first read Ephesians, or heard it read, this language might have recalled the effusive language used in inscriptions recognizing the benefactions of emperors of the Augustan age. Here too forms of the verb ὑπερβάλλω (hyperballō) were used to describe the emperor’s εὔνοια (eunoia, goodwill), φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpia, benevolence), ἀνδρεία (andreia, courage), φιλοδοξία (philodoxia, love of fame), φιλοτιμία (philotimia, love of honor), μεγαλοφροσύνη (megalophrosynē, greatness of mind), σωφροσύνη (sōphrosynē, moderation), ἀρετή (aretē, merit), and φιλοτειμία προγονική (philoteimia progonikē, ancestral honor), all of them specific manifestations of the emperor’s χάρις (Harrison 2003: 231n73; Whitlark 2003).

The three prepositional phrases—ἐν τοῖς αἰῶσιν τοῖς ἐπερχομένοις (en tois aiōsin tois eperchomenois, in the coming ages), ἐν χρηστότητι (en chrēstotēti, by kindness), and ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (en Christō Iēsou, in Christ Jesus)—all modify the verb ἐνδείξηται and describe three different elements of God’s demonstration of his surpassing grace.

First, ἐν τοῖς αἰῶσιν τοῖς ἐπερχομένοις describes how long this demonstration will last. A few interpreters have linked this phrase with the interpretation of αἰῶν in 2:2 and 3:9–10 as a personal power and claimed that Paul (or the author) thought of God as displaying to “the attacking Aeons” his graciousness to his people.[21] Paul’s reference to “the [age] to come” (τῷ μέλλοντι [αἰῶνι], tō mellonti [aiōni]) in 1:21 and the use of the phrase ὁ αἰὼν ὁ ἐπερχόμενος (ho aiōn ho eperchomenos) elsewhere (Mark 10:30; Herm. Vis. 4.3.5) clearly to mean “the coming age,” however, make this idea unlikely.[22] Paul intends to say that God has saved believers so that he might show his surpassing grace to them in all future ages.

Second, the phrase ἐν χρηστότητι ἐφ᾿ ἡμᾶς (en chrēstotēti eph’ hēmas, by kindness toward us) tells Paul’s readers how God will display his grace. The term χρηστότης (chrēstotēs, kindness) appears commonly in Jewish and Christian literature as an attribute that God exercises “toward” (ἐπί, epi) his people (e.g., Pss. Sol. 5.18; 9.7; 18.1; Rom. 11:22; cf. 2:4; Titus 3:4). When the word is used of God in the LXX of the Psalms, it stands parallel to his mercy (ἔλεος, eleos; 24:7 [25:7 MT, Eng.]; 118:65 [119:65 MT, Eng.]), his righteousness (δικαιοσύνη, dikaiosynē; 144:7 [145:7 MT, Eng.]), and his willingness to help the erring by teaching them his commandments (118:68 [119:68 MT, Eng.]). In other literature, the word is often associated with a mildness (ἡμερότης, hēmerotēs), charitable disposition (κοινωνία, koinōnia), magnanimity (μεγαλόνοια, megalonoia), benevolence (φιλανθρωπία, philanthrōpia), and even cheerfulness (εὐθυμία, euthymia), which fits the temperament of God toward his people as Paul describes it in the opening benedictory prayer (1:5–8).[23]

Third, the phrase ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (en Christō Iēsou, in Christ Jesus) describes the sphere in which God’s grace and kindness work on behalf of his people. In the context of 2:5–6, Paul probably has in mind especially the identity of believers with Christ in his life, resurrection, and position with God in heaven.

Summary

In 2:4–7 Paul paints a bright portrait of God’s grace that stands in dramatic contrast to the dark landscape of human sin in 2:1–3. By giving believers life with Christ, raising them with Christ, and seating them with Christ in his place of victory, God has demonstrated the overwhelmingly merciful, loving, and gracious nature of his character. This demonstration of his character was not something that happened as a side effect of his gracious saving work, but was the very purpose for which he did this work. He rescued those who are in Christ from the domination of the world, the devil, and the flesh so that he might demonstrate forever the overwhelmingly gracious nature of his character.



Additional Note

2:5. Two textual problems arise here in close proximity to one another. First, some manuscripts of primarily the Alexandrian text type (𝔓46, B, 33) and some Western witnesses among the versions and Fathers (a few Old Latin manuscripts, Victorinus of Rome, Ambrose) place the preposition ἐν in front of the phrase τῷ Χριστῷ (συνεζωοποίησεν ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ). If this were correct, it would be exegetically significant since συνεζωοποίησεν would then refer not to the union of Christians with Christ’s new life but to the union of Christians whom, together, God had made alive “in Christ.” It might then anticipate the theme of the unity of Gentile and Jewish Christians in 2:11–22.

The concentration of the manuscripts with this reading in the Alexandrian text type and the lateness of the Western witnesses, however, make this reading a poor choice in comparison to the simple τῷ Χριστῷ, which appears in early Alexandrian (א, A) as well as Western (D, F, G) and Byzantine witnesses (L, and a range of minuscules).[24] The additional ἐν arose either as an echo of ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ at the end of 2:6, or (more probably, since the phrase in 2:6 comes later) from a mistaken repetition of the final syllable of the preceding συνεζωοποίησεν.

Second, the reading χάριτι immediately after τῷ Χριστῷ appears in the Alexandrian manuscripts 𝔓46, א, B, and in many Byzantine manuscripts. It therefore has early and wide attestation and is, with the highest probability and with virtually no controversy, the correct reading. The two variations from this reading come from late manuscripts, and each is limited to a single text type. They are interesting mainly because they seem to show how grammatically difficult some native Greek speakers found Paul’s outburst about the grace of God. A number of late, Byzantine manuscripts (e.g., 256, 365, 436, 1319, 1573, 2127) have χάριτι γάρ. This would have approximated the grammar of 2:8 (τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι) and smoothed out the sentence slightly (“he made us alive together with Christ, for you are saved by grace”). Two ninth-century uncial manuscripts with a Western text type (F, G) have οὗ χάριτι, and D has οὗ τῇ χάριτι.[25] Here too the concern may have been to attach χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι somehow to its grammatical context (“he made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you are saved”).[26]





IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)

A. Children of Wrath Like All the Rest (2:1–3)

B. Objects of God’s Mercy (2:4–7)

C. The Nature and Consequences of God’s Grace (2:8–10)


C. The Nature and Consequences of God’s Grace (2:8–10)

Paul now explains in greater detail the grace that he had mentioned briefly in 2:5 and that provides the foundation for the saved status of his readers. Their present existence as people who have been made alive together with Christ (2:5), who have been raised with him, and who have been enthroned with him in heavenly places (2:6)—this existence is entirely a product of that grace. Its foundational importance, therefore, demands further explanation.

In various ways throughout the paragraph, Paul emphasizes that the salvation he has just described in 2:4–7 came entirely at God’s initiative and as a free gift. The vocabulary he uses brings out the utterly free nature of salvation: Paul describes it as an act of “grace” (χάρις, charis) and as a “gift” (δῶρον, dōron). It is received “through faith” (διὰ πίστεως, dia pisteōs), and for Paul, this means that no meritorious human effort was involved. Even the good works that arise as a consequence of salvation, and that Paul and his readers should do, God “prepared beforehand” (προητοίμασεν, proētoimasen), presumably from before the foundation of the world.

Paul’s syntax works toward the same goal. When Paul says that God’s grace has saved his readers, he positions the term “grace” near the front of the clause (as he had already done in v. 5) to give it special emphasis. In addition, when he says that salvation is the gift of God, he places the word “God” before the word “gift” to put the emphasis on God (θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον, theou to dōron, God’s gift). Similarly, in his description of himself and his readers as God’s creation, he puts the possessive pronoun (αὐτοῦ, autou, his) first in the clause to make clear that “we are his handiwork.”

The paragraph can be divided into two parts. First, in 2:8–9 Paul describes the completely free nature of salvation and concludes from it that no one can boast. The implication is clear: the only appropriate boasting in connection with salvation must be a boast in God for what he has done for those who are saved. This not only recalls the frequent concern with boasting in the theology of the undisputed Pauline letters (Gal. 6:14; 1 Cor. 1:26–31; 4:7; Phil. 3:3; 2 Cor. 5:12; 12:9–10; Rom. 3:27; 4:1–2; 5:2–3) but also picks up the threefold claim in the benediction that God included Paul and his readers among his people by his grace and to the praise of his glory (Eph. 1:6, 12, 14). If Paul’s readers do not understand that their salvation is entirely God’s doing, with no contribution from themselves, then God will fail to receive from them the glory that is rightfully his.

Second, in 2:10 Paul tells his readers that he and they were created by God for the purpose of doing the good works that God prepared in advance for them to do. The completely gracious nature of salvation does not mean that Paul and his readers are passive creatures but that they are new creations and should accomplish what God, their re-creator, designed them to do. By introducing this ethical theme and expressing it in the language of a new creation (cf. 2 Cor. 5:17; Gal. 6:15), Paul prevents any misunderstanding that the gracious nature of salvation implies that believers “should do evil that good may come” (Rom. 3:8; cf. 6:1, 15). He also prepares his readers for the development of the new-creation theme in the next section (2:15) and for the ethical implications of the theme he brings out in the second main part of the letter (4:13, 22, 24).

Despite the shift of attention to the “good works” that believers do, Paul continues to emphasize God’s gracious initiative. Even when they live in the way God created them to live, Paul and his readers remain God’s creation and are only doing the good works that God prepared long ago for them to accomplish. Thus, the praise even for their good works goes to God.

Paul ends this second part of the paragraph, and with it the entire section (2:1–10), with language that recalls the human plight outside of Christ as he described it in 2:1–3. In this way, he emphasizes the stark contrast between what he and his readers once were and what God has now made of them. In 2:1–3 he said that his readers used to “walk” (περιπατέω, peripateō) “in” (ἐν, en) transgressions and sins (vv. 1–2). He now says that when God rescued them from this desperate plight, he re-created them and put them on a new ethical path: they now should “walk” (περιπατέω) “in” (ἐν) the good works he intended them to do from before the foundation of the world.



Exegesis and Exposition

8aFor by that grace you are saved, through faith; 8band this is not from yourselves; 9it is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one might boast. 10For we are his handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand in order that we might walk in them.

[2:8a] The first sentence of the new section shows why (γάρ, gar, for) God is able to demonstrate his gracious character throughout eternity to Paul and his readers. Paul states the reason in language that repeats the wording of his brief outburst about God’s grace in 2:5 (χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι, chariti este sesōmenoi), but with two significant additions. Each addition emphasizes the foundational importance of God’s grace to the set of events that brought them salvation.

First, he adds the article before the word χάριτι and in this way points back to “that” grace of which he spoke in 2:5 and 7 (Wallace 1996: 250). That grace united Paul and his readers with Christ, making them alive with Christ and seating them with Christ in heavenly places (i.e., it “saved” them). Because (γάρ) God united them with the enthroned Christ by his grace and will show his grace to them for eternity, it is indeed by grace that they are saved.[1]

Second, Paul adds that on the human side, salvation comes “through” the response of “faith” (διὰ πίστεως, dia pisteōs). God offers salvation to his human creatures abundantly and freely, but as Paul implies in Rom. 5:17, they must “receive” it. They must trust God that his free provision for them in Christ will actually accomplish their salvation (cf. Rom. 3:24–25; 4:19–22). For the readers of Ephesians, this means trusting “the word of truth, the gospel of [their] salvation” (1:13; cf. 1:19).

It did not mean, as Theodoret thought, that Paul’s readers “had only faith to offer, but divine grace worked with it” (R. Hill 2001: 2.39). In Paul’s thinking, faith is not something that people offer to God and with which God’s grace then cooperates to save them. Rather, faith is aligned with grace, and both faith and grace stand over against anything that human beings can offer God: it is neither a work deserving payment nor a ground for boasting (Rom. 4:2–5, 16). To say that salvation comes “through faith,” therefore, is to further enhance the notion that it arises from the grace of God (Haupt 1902a: 65).

[2:8b–9] Paul makes this theme explicit in his next two statements, each of which contrasts the impotence of human nature and activity with God’s generosity and glory in salvation. The first statement (v. 8b) denies that “this” (τοῦτο, touto) salvation of which Paul has just spoken arose from anything within Paul’s readers (ἐξ ὑμῶν, ex hymōn).[2] How could it? They were “dead in transgressions and sins” (v. 1; cf. v. 5a) and were “by nature children of wrath” (v. 3). Their salvation, therefore, had to come as God’s δῶρον (dōron, gift).[3]

The second statement (v. 9) denies that salvation comes “from” any “works” they might accomplish (ἐξ ἔργων, ex ergōn). Prior to their conversion, “the Ruler of the realm of the air” was powerfully at work (ἐνεργοῦντος, energountos) in them, and they followed the cravings of their fallen flesh and mind (vv. 2–3). Accomplishing their own salvation, therefore, was impossible. God’s purpose in arranging salvation as his accomplishment alone was ἵνα μή τις καυχήσηται (hina mē tis kauchēsētai, so that no one might boast). This seems to be an allusive way of saying, “so that all might boast in God alone.” The thought is similar to the line of argument in Rom. 4–5. If Abraham were justified before God “from” his “works” (ἐξ ἔργων), Paul says, he has a ground for boasting (Rom. 4:2; cf. 3:27; 4:6; 11:6). Since justification comes by faith, however, the “boasting” (καυχώμενοι, kauchōmenoi) of the believer must be “in God” (ἐν τῷ θεῷ, en tō theō; Rom. 5:11).

Still, Rom. 4–5 differs from Eph. 2:8–9 in its use of the verb “justify” to describe what God has done for us and in its location within an argument that speaks not simply of human works generally but also of “works of the [Jewish] law” (3:20, 27–28; 9:12, 32; cf. Gal. 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10). Moreover, as with Eph. 2:5–6, here salvation is a present reality, not something whose completion lies in the future as it does in Rom. 5:9–10. Does this mean that Ephesians comes from a time long after the ethnic tension between Jewish and Gentile Christians had been resolved (Luz 1976: 372; 1998: 134; Lincoln 1983: 627–28)? Had the imminent expectation of the eschatological judgment of God faded and the theological accent in the Pauline school shifted from apocalyptically laden notions of justification and God’s righteousness to general expressions of God’s grace and of a salvation already accomplished (Luz 1976: 372)?

As with Eph. 2:5–6, there is again no compelling reason to travel this road. On one hand, the Paul of the undisputed letters can insist, outside of any struggle with Judaizing tendencies, that God’s call and choice of the “foolish,” the “weak,” the “low,” and the “nothings” of the world excludes human boasting (1 Cor. 1:26–30). He can ask the haughty and divided Corinthians, “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast [καυχᾶσαι, kauchasai] as if you did not receive it?” (1 Cor. 4:7b). On the other hand, the Paul of Ephesians, in the climactic passage on the armor of God (6:10–17), can direct Christians to take “up the shield of faith” (v. 16) and to “receive the helmet of salvation” (v. 17) in light of the current struggle that they have with the “world rulers of this darkness” (v. 12). This assumes that salvation and faith, although in one sense accomplished gifts of God for the believer, must nevertheless be constantly appropriated in light of the present onslaught of evil.

The precise combination of words in Eph. 2:8–9 is certainly unusual: the Paul of the undisputed letters uses the language of “works” and the language of “boasting” together only when engaging Judaism polemically.[4] Still, the thought of Eph. 2:8–9 is Pauline, and it is not hard to imagine Paul expressing himself this way in a new setting. There is, moreover, some precedent for a redefinition of “works” in terms solely of human effort generally (rather than specifically Jewish effort to keep the law) in Rom. 4:1–8, where the discussion focuses on the “works” of Abraham and David rather than specifically on their obedience to the Jewish law (cf. Rom. 9:11–12; 11:6; I. Marshall 1996: 345n21).

[2:10] Paul’s next statement performs three functions. First, it gives the reason why Paul can say that salvation, in its entirety, is a gift of God: God created Paul and his readers anew. Second, by introducing this theme, it foreshadows the motif of the new creation that will play such an important role in the next section (2:14–15; cf. 4:13, 22, 24). Third, it brings 2:1–10 to a fitting close by implicitly contrasting the way Paul’s readers used to “walk” (2:2) and the way that both he and they now “walk,” thanks to God’s gracious, saving work.

The salvation of Paul and his readers is entirely God’s gift because (γάρ, gar) they are God’s ποίημα (poiēma, creation).[5] The term ποιήμα can mean “artifact,” “poem,” or “literary production in prose” as well as simply “what is done” (LSJ 1429; LSJSup 253; BDAG 842). Its only other use in the Pauline corpus (indeed the NT), however, refers to the “works” (ποιήματα, poiēmata) of God at creation (Rom. 1:20). As Paul’s next two clauses show, this is also how he uses the term here.[6] Paul’s placement of the pronoun αὐτοῦ (autou, his) at the beginning of the clause is intentional and emphatic (Robinson 1934: 681; MHT 3:190). He wants to emphasize that the refashioning of people who were once dead in transgressions and sins and by nature children of wrath (2:1, 3) into a spiritually alive people, victorious over the evil cosmic powers ranged against them (2:4–6), is entirely a work of God. “We are,” he says, “his creation.”

The idea that Christians are part of a new, eschatological creation appears in the undisputed letters (Gal. 6:15; 2 Cor. 5:17) and plays a role in the ethical admonitions in Colossians (3:10), where the theme of Christ as the agent of the original creation is prominent (1:15, 23). In Ephesians too, Christ is the agent of the new creation (2:15b), and the idea of a new creation lays the groundwork for some of the letter’s ethical admonitions in its second section (4:13, 22, 24).

Perhaps with a side glance at the misunderstanding that sometimes plagued his theology of grace (Rom. 3:8; 6:1, 15; James 2:14–26; Jude 4; cf. 2 Pet. 3:15–17),[7] the apostle now asserts that good works are both integral to the existence of the people God has created and are themselves the products of God’s gracious initiative on behalf of his people (cf. 1 Cor. 15:10). Christians were created ἐπὶ ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς (epi ergois agathois, for the purpose of good works).

Interpreters often comment on the un-Pauline nature of the expression ἔργα ἀγαθά (erga agatha, good works).[8] The Paul of the undisputed letters can certainly speak in various ways of “doing good” (Gal. 6:10; 2 Cor. 9:8; Rom. 2:7, 10; 13:3; cf. Phil. 1:6), but within the Pauline corpus generally, the plural expression “good works” appears only in the Pastorals, letters whose Pauline authorship is disputed (1 Tim. 2:10; 5:10, 25; 6:18; Titus 2:7, 14; 3:8, 14).[9] This stylistic difference from the undisputed letters, however, is counterbalanced to some extent by the use of the expression as the object of a prepositional phrase using ἐπί and the dative to express purpose. The three NT appearances of this idiom belong to the Pauline corpus, and the thought of 1 Thess. 4:7, where it is also used, is close to the thought here (cf. Gal. 5:13; 2 Tim. 2:14).[10]

The point, in any case, is clear. God intended those whom he has saved by his abundant grace to live in the way later described in 4:1–6:20. These “good works” are neither the basis of salvation nor, as F. C. Baur (2003: 2.39–40) thought, given equal status with faith by a post-Pauline writer more in line theologically with James than with Paul. As the aorist participle κτισθέντες (ktisthentes, created) shows, this sentence conceives of good works as the consequence of a new creation that has already taken place (Haupt 1902a: 67–68; cf. Alford 1857: 92; Ellicott 1859: 42).

To keep the emphasis on God’s gracious initiative, moreover, Paul speaks of God preparing beforehand (προητοίμασεν, proētoimasen) the works in which he intended his people to walk.[11] The term προετοιμάζω (proetoimazō) was used to refer to the thoughtful preparation of something: a “previously prepared supper” (τὸ προητοιμασμένον . . . δεῖπνον, to proētoimasmenon . . . deipnon; Pseudo-Plutarch, Apoph. lac. 230 E), for example, or accusations in a legal case “prepared beforehand” (τὰ . . . προητοιμασμένα, ta . . . proētoimasmena; Josephus, Ant. 17.121). In Hellenistic Jewish literature, it could be used in a theological context to refer to God’s preparation, at the creation of the world, for people and institutions that would come later (Wis. 9:8; Philo, Creation 77), or, as in its only other NT use, God’s preparation of a people “for glory” (Rom. 9:23). The good works that God’s people will do, therefore, have all been planned since the beginning of the world, just as the blessing of God’s people and his plan for the universe were carefully determined “beforehand.”[12] Therefore, even when believers “walk worthily of the calling with which” they were called (4:1), they have nothing to boast about before God: in this, too, God took the initiative by carefully preparing these good works before the foundation of the world.

Paul concludes with a comment on God’s purpose in preparing these good works: he did so “in order that we might walk [περιπατήσωμεν, peripatēsōmen] in them.” With this phrase Paul makes clear that Christians must accomplish what God has prepared in advance for them to do. The use of the term περιπατέω (peripateō) for the first time since 2:2 leads Paul’s readers back to the beginning of the passage and neatly concludes the entire section by offering a dramatic contrast between its beginning and its end. Paul’s readers no longer walk in sin, according to the standards of the world and the prince of the demonic realm, but in the way carefully planned by the Creator for his creation from a time before the world began. The theme of the ethical plan the Creator intends his newly created people to fulfill prepares the way for the further development of the “new humanity” theme in the next section (2:11–22). It also foreshadows the long section of ethical instructions (4:1–6:20), with its frequent use of the verb περιπατέω (walk; 4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15) and its use of the new creation theme as an incentive for ethical behavior (4:13, 22, 24).

Summary

In 2:8–10 Paul further defines the overwhelming graciousness of God. He does this by affirming that the work of salvation belongs solely to God, who grants salvation as an entirely free gift and emphatically not on the basis of human effort. The human response of faith to this gift, far from constituting anything for which a human being can take credit, excludes by its very nature any element of human boasting. Those who receive this entirely free gift of God’s salvation, however, do not remain unchanged. God re-creates them so that they do the work he planned for his people to do before the creation of the world.

With this final subsection of 2:1–10, Paul brings to a close his treatment of how God’s great power in raising Christ from the dead and seating him in a position of victory at his right hand works for the benefit of the individual believer. God has rescued those who are in Christ from the desperate plight of sinful rebellion against God and subservience to the devil by uniting them with Christ in his new life and position of victory over the enemy forces of the transcendent realm. He has re-created them so that they now walk not in transgressions, sins, the course of the world, the evil desires of their minds, and in fealty to the devil, but as God created human beings to live from the beginning. God has done this in such a way that by it he has demonstrated the lavishly gracious nature of his character.





IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)

V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)

VI. Paul’s Divinely Given Task and His Suffering for the Gentiles (3:1–13)

VII. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength and Praises the God Who Can Give It (3:14–21)


V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)

In 2:11–22 Paul explains how the mighty power that God demonstrated in Christ (1:19) affects believers as a people (Best 1998: 235; Hoehner 2002: 305, 351; Aletti 2001: 113). The passage roughly follows the pattern of 2:1–10 (cf. O’Brien 1999: 183). It begins with a description of the plight of existence without God (vv. 11–12; cf. vv. 1–3) and then explains the divine response to that plight (vv. 13–18; cf. vv. 4–8). It ends with a description of the positive implications that God’s response to the human plight has for present existence (vv. 19–22; cf. v. 10). The syntax of both passages is also similar. Both passages move from human plight to divine solution by posing a contrast between what “once” was and what “now” is (cf. Tachau 1972: 134–42), although in 2:1–10 the scheme is less explicit than it is in 2:11–22 (Lincoln 1990: 124). In both passages Paul also explains God’s response to the plight in syntax that becomes difficult and broken (vv. 14–15a; cf. vv. 5b–6).

Despite these similarities, the two passages have important thematic differences. Whereas 2:1–10 focused on the plight of every human being without mention of ethnic or social tension (vv. 1–3), 2:11–22 now speaks of the special plight of the Gentiles as a people estranged from God because of their alienation from Israel (vv. 11–12). Whereas 2:1–10 emphasized the believer’s union with Christ in his resurrection and ascension, providing a clear example of how God’s powerful work in resurrecting Christ benefits Christians (1:19–21), 2:11–22 now emphasizes Christ’s death as the divine solution (vv. 14–18).[1]

In short, the primary orientation of 2:1–10 is vertical, and the primary orientation of 2:11–22 is horizontal (cf. Aletti 2001: 113). The focus of 2:1–10 is God’s powerful work through Christ’s resurrection and ascension to orient the individual human believer away from the world, the devil, and the flesh and toward the Creator. The focus of 2:11–22 is the social alienation between Israel and the Gentiles and Christ’s role in solving this problem through his death, which set aside the Mosaic law, with its tendency to divide Jews from Gentiles. Although the death of Christ also overcomes the hostility between God and humanity, this element of the passage serves the passage’s more prominent theme of the peace that now exists between Jews and Gentiles. By overcoming the hostility between God and all human beings, Christ’s death breaks down the wall of hostility between Jews and Gentiles.

The basic orientation of the two passages is evident in the different ways they use words compounded with the preposition σύν (syn, with). In 2:1–10 these compounds are oriented vertically, referring to the believer’s union with Christ in his position of heavenly victory, but in 2:11–22 they are oriented horizontally, referring to the union of Gentile believers with their Jewish counterparts in God’s household:

Ephesians 2:1–10 (vertically oriented) Ephesians 2:11–22 (horizontally oriented)



* * *





συνεζωοποίησεν (synezōpoiēsen, made alive together with; v. 5) συμπολῖται (sympolitai, citizens together with; v. 19)



* * *





συνήγειρεν (synēgeiren, raised together with; v. 6) συναρμολογουμένη (synarmologoumenē, joined together; v. 21)



* * *





συνεκάθισεν (synekathisen, seated together with; v. 6) συνοικοδομεῖσθε (synoikodomeisthe, you are being built together; v. 22)



* * *





If we turn to the internal structure of the passage, we find that the primary theme of peace between Israel and the Gentiles and the subsidiary theme of peace with God progress together in three steps. In the first step (2:11–13) Paul describes the ethnic tension that has existed between his Gentile readers and the Jews with their special society, their way of life, and the promise in their Scriptures of the Messiah, or as he is called in Greek, ὁ Χριστός (ho Christos, the Christ). This alienation was so serious not merely because of the social tensions involved but also, as the final item in Paul’s description of the plight reveals, because the social tension was closely bound up with the Gentiles’ plight of being “without God in the world” (v. 12; cf. vv. 1–3). Paul concludes the first step by announcing God’s solution to the especially bleak plight of his Gentile readers. God has brought them near: near to himself and near to each other “in Christ,” and “by means of his blood” (v. 13). This concluding statement provides a springboard for the second step in the development of his theme.

The second step (vv. 14–18) explores precisely how Christ’s death brought “peace” (vv. 14, 15, 17) to a divided humanity and to a humanity divided from God. The spotlight now falls on Christ himself rather than on God’s action through Christ, and Paul shifts from speaking to his readers as a separate group (“you Gentiles,” v. 11) to including himself, although a Jew, with them (“He himself is our peace,” v. 14). Paul explains that the death of Christ on the cross tore down the dividing wall (the Mosaic law) that enclosed the Jews and separated them from the Gentiles. In the hands of sinful human beings, the law had become an instrument of hostility, but when Christ’s death set it aside, he created in himself one new, undivided human being. Sinful human beings had also used the Mosaic law as an instrument of hostility against God (cf. Rom. 4:15; 5:20; 7:5, 7–8, 11), and the death of Christ also solved this problem for both Jews and Gentiles.

Following the same method he had adopted at the conclusion of the first step (v. 13), Paul closes this second step in a way that provides a springboard to the third step. Believing Jews and Gentiles, he says, now have access to God as “Father” (v. 18), and this thought provides a skillful transition to the theme of God’s “household,” which dominates the third step in his argument.

This third step (vv. 19–22), with its progressive imagery of God’s people as “household,” “building,” and “dwelling place,” fully resolves the plight that Paul laid out in the first step (vv. 11–12). The tension and estrangement between Israel and the Gentiles and between the Gentiles and God has disappeared. Paul’s Gentile readers are now part of the society of God’s people, part of the household over which God presides as Father (v. 19), part of a firmly founded, tightly fitted building currently under construction (vv. 20–21a). Indeed, Paul says climactically, they help form the temple in which God’s Spirit dwells (vv. 21b–22). In all this, they participate as “citizens together” with all the saints, whether Jewish or Gentile, because they are now part of a new people of God in which ethnic and national divisions have disappeared.

The theme of God’s people as members of his household, which echoes throughout the passage in the repetition of words built on the syllable -οἰκ- (-oik-, -hous-; this syllable appears six times), both reaches back to the important statement in 1:10, where the term οἰκονομία (oikonomia, administration) occurs, and forward toward the use of this same term in 3:2, 9. Most fundamentally, this term means “management of a household” (LSJ 1204), and it probably continues to carry something of its original sense into these three metaphorical uses.[2] Paul may have been thinking of the universe as a household, and then alternately of God as the Father who administers the universe according to his will (1:10) and of himself as one who has the responsibility of carrying out the administrative plans of the Father (3:2, 9), much like a slave might serve as an administrator of household affairs on a large estate (cf. Luke 16:2–4). Perhaps in 2:19–22 Paul develops the metaphor of God’s people as members of God’s household and as the building or dwelling place of God in order to remind his readers that the church has played an important role in God’s administration of the entire universe.





V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)

A. The Special Plight of the Gentiles and God’s Response (2:11–13)

B. Christ Is the Believing Community’s Peace (2:14–18)

C. Gentile Christians as an Integral Part of God’s Household (2:19–22)


A. The Special Plight of the Gentiles and God’s Response (2:11–13)

Paul now advances his discussion of how “the surpassing greatness of God’s power” (1:19) has affected his readers by speaking to them for the first time specifically as non-Jews (2:11). All people, Jews as well as Gentiles, stood under the terrible plight that Paul described in 2:1–3, and all believers, whether Jew or Gentile, have been rescued from that plight by the gracious, divine initiative Paul has just described in 2:4–10. Gentiles, however, were at a special disadvantage and should, accordingly, appreciate God’s grace all the more. In 2:11–13, Paul outlines this specifically Gentile plight and then states God’s solution to it in a concise way that prepares for a fuller development of it in 2:14–18 and 19–22.

The passage can be divided into two parts, the first describing what the Gentiles were “once” (v. 11) and “at that time” (v. 12), and the second explaining what has “now” happened to them (v. 13). The first part can also be divided into two parts. First, in 2:11 Paul describes the Gentiles’ separation from Israel in physical and negative terms from the perspective of Judaism: Gentiles were “called ‘foreskin’” by the Jews because they lacked circumcision, a physical marker recognized by both Jew and Gentile as distinctive of Judaism. The note of ethnic tension Paul sounds here prepares for the divine solution to this tension in the next section (vv. 14–15).

Second, in 2:12 Paul lists five theological disadvantages of the Gentiles, and all except the last, summative item (“without God in the world”) are related to the Gentiles’ lack of access to the Scriptures. Because Israel’s Scriptures contain the promise of the Messiah and outline the way of life God expected his people to follow, Gentiles were left on their own, without real hope or guidance, a fate that we know from 2:1–3 placed them at the mercy of the world, the devil, and the flesh (cf. 4:17–19).

Despite its concern to show the theological advantages that belong to Israel, this passage is written from a Christian rather than a Jewish perspective. This is apparent in the last phrases of 2:11, with their negative evaluation of physical circumcision, and in the orientation of the list of Gentile disadvantages toward the Christian hope and promise of a Messiah in 2:12. The perspective is historical: 2:12 describes the sad state of Gentiles, when compared with Israel, prior to the coming of the gospel (Lincoln 1987: 615–17; 1990: 136).

Does this mean, as Lincoln (1987: 619–20; 1990: 134) has argued, that the passage comes from a post-Pauline period, when the separation of the church from the synagogue was a fait accompli and the ardor of Paul’s anguish over the irony of Israel’s unbelief had long since cooled? MacDonald has correctly called this approach to the passage into question because it does not accurately reflect the post-Pauline situation. The late first century, she argues, appears to have been a time when some Christians sought to emphasize the Jewish character of their religion in order to avoid persecution (MacDonald 2004: 434–37).

If this was true of the late first century, however, it was also true of the mid-first century. Paul’s Judaizing opponents in Galatia tried to compel the Gentile Galatian Christians to accept circumcision, he says, “only in order that they might not be persecuted for the cross of Christ” (Gal. 6:12). This may well have been an effort to avoid harassment by local magistrates through seeking the protection of Judaism.[1] In 2:11–13 Paul walks the tightrope of both affirming that all who have believed the gospel are indebted to Judaism and, at the same time, insisting that believers are now part of a new people not limited by ethnic boundaries.



Exegesis and Exposition

11Therefore remember that once you Gentiles in the flesh—those called “foreskin” by the so-called ⌜circumcision⌝ (⌜done by hand⌝ in the flesh)—12that you were, at that time, outside Christ, alienated from Israel’s way of life and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. 13But now, in Christ Jesus, you who were once far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.

[2:11] Paul connects this new stage in his argument with the previous stage by means of the particle διό (dio, therefore). Διό normally draws an inference, sometimes from the immediately preceding statement (e.g., 4:8; 5:14), and sometimes from the preceding paragraph (e.g., 3:13). As with 3:13, Paul here draws an inference from all that he has said in 2:1–10: if God has graciously saved all who have faith in Christ from the world, the devil, and the flesh and has re-created them so that they do the good works God originally created humanity to do, then his Gentile readers should especially recall how far they have come. Later Paul will say that their former way of life as Gentiles was characterized by futility, darkness, alienation from God, ignorance, hard-heartedness, despondency, and extreme immorality (4:17–19). Here in 2:11, Paul urges them to “continue to remember” (μνημονεύετε, mnēmoneuete) what they “once” (ποτέ, pote) were as Gentiles as a way of further appreciating the magnitude of God’s powerful work on their behalf.

Paul describes what they once were in two ways, each introduced with a ὅτι (hoti) recitative (“that”): first (here in v. 11) he explains how Jews defined Gentiles, and second (in v. 12) he describes the privileges from which they were excluded since they did not belong to Israel (v. 12).[2]

First, then, Paul says that his readers did not have the physical mark of circumcision, which distinguished Jews from Gentiles. They were Gentiles ἐν σαρκί (en sarki, in the flesh) and were called ἀκροβυστία (akrobystia, foreskin) by the Jews. Paul’s language echoes the LXX version of Gen. 17:11–12, where God tells Abraham to “be circumcised [plural] in the foreskin of your flesh” (LXX, περιτμηθήσεσθε τὴν σάρκα τῆς ἀκροβυστίας, peritmēthēsesthe tēn sarka tēs akrobystias) as a sign of the covenant between God and his descendants (cf. Jdt. 14:10; Sir. 44:20). Non-Jews, therefore, were literally “Gentiles in the flesh,” for their males retained their “foreskin.” The term λεγόμενοι (legomenoi, called) hints that ἀκροβυστία was used derisively and emphasizes the tension that existed between Jews and Gentiles over precisely this physical distinction between them (see the additional note). Paul’s point, then, is that the Jews saw the Gentiles as excluded from their social group and therefore from the special relationship with God of which circumcision was the outward, physical marker.

Paul tells us that Jews, in contrast, are ἡ λεγομένη περιτομή (hē legomenē peritomē), “the so-called circumcision.” Paul could mean this in either of two ways: (1) in the neutral sense that this is what they call themselves (Best 1998: 239; Muddiman 2001: 117),[3] or (2) in the negative sense that, despite their claim of being “the circumcision,” they are not really circumcised since true circumcision is spiritual rather than physical (Ellicott 1859: 43; Abbott 1897: 56; Eadie 1883: 162; cf. Rom. 2:28–29; 3:3). Since Paul goes on to describe physical circumcision with the negative term χειροποίητος (cheiropoiētos, done by hand; see the additional note on this term), he probably also intends the adjectival participle λεγομένη negatively.

Real circumcision, Paul explains in Col. 2:11–12, is “not done by hand” (ἀχειροποίητος, acheiropoiētos) but involves identification with Christ’s death. That means physical circumcision is only an operation done in the flesh (Phil. 3:2–3; Rom. 2:28–29). It is significant as a “sign” and “seal” of faith for Jewish Christians (Rom. 4:11), but in no way is it necessary for membership in God’s people (Rom. 4:16; cf. Gal. 6:15; 1 Cor. 6:19).

Why does Paul introduce a note of distance between Christians and Jews precisely in a place where he is trying to remind his Gentile Christian readers that the Jews were closer to God than they had been as unbelieving Gentiles? The way Paul shapes his language here has to do with his historical presuppositions. Prior to the gospel’s entrance onto the scene, the Jews had enormous religious advantages over the Gentiles, advantages that Paul will list in the next verse, but after the gospel’s advent and the inclusion of Gentiles within God’s newly constituted people, these advantages were overshadowed by the rejection of the gospel among most Jews and their perpetuation of social distinctions that God, through the gospel, had abolished.[4] Even as Paul reminds his readers of their exclusion from historical Israel, with its close relationship to God, therefore, he hints that Israel, although historically “near” to God, nevertheless needs to be reconciled to him through faith in the gospel (2:16–17).[5]

[2:12] Paul now backs up to the main verb μνημονεύετε and launches the second part of his description of his readers’ specifically Gentile plight. As Gentiles, they were deprived of five advantages in comparison with Israel, the people from whom, according to verse 11, they were excluded.

1. They were χωρὶς Χριστοῦ (chōris christou, outside Christ). This is the most important item in the list, as its position indicates: it is at the head of the list, outside the two couplets (each linked with καί [kai, and]) used to express the other four problems. If every spiritual blessing of 1:4–12 is available only to those “in Christ” (1:3), and if rescue from the grim plight detailed in 2:1–3 comes only to those “in Christ” (2:5–6), then being “outside Christ” poses a problem of the first rank. Since Christ was not yet present in any clear way in biblical Israel, Paul speaks here of the promise of the Messiah in Israel’s Scriptures (cf. Rom. 9:5).[6]

What Scriptures might these be? Later he will say that Gentiles were alienated from “the covenants of promise,” and the line of thought he develops in Gal. 3:16 and 29, where God’s covenant promise to Abraham concerns the Messiah (cf. Gen. 13:15; 15:18; 17:8; 24:7), may be in the background.[7] Regardless of the precise allusion, his primary point is reasonably clear: prior to the gospel, Gentiles were separated from the hope that Jews had in the coming of the Messiah, a hope that was eventually fulfilled in Jesus.[8]

2. Unbelieving Gentiles were also ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς πολιτείας τοῦ Ἰσραήλ (apēllotriōmenoi tēs politeias tou Israēl, alienated from Israel’s way of life). The verb ἀπαλλοτριόω (apallotrioō, alienate) refers to separation—of people from their property if they sell it (Aristotle, Rhet. 1.5.7; I. Magnesia Sip. 19 [NewDocs 3:24]), of wives from husbands (1 Clem. 6.3), of people from God (Col. 1:21), and in Ephesians, specifically of Gentiles from the life that God gives (Eph. 4:18; see LSJ 176; BDAG 96). The perfect participle functions as an adjectival predicate of ἦτε (etē, you were), like the adjective ξένοι (xenoi, strangers) in the next clause (ἦτε . . . ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι . . . καὶ ξένοι, ēte . . . apēllotriōmenoi . . . kai xenoi, you were . . . alienated . . . and strangers), not as part of a periphrastic construction.[9] This probably means that we should not find too many nuances either in the lexical meaning of ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι or in its tense. The term basically means here what ξένοι means in the next clause. Prior to the intervention of the gospel, Gentiles were separated from, or “strangers to,” the πολιτεία (politeia) of Israel.

But what does πολιτεία mean? Traditionally, commentators have understood it in one of three ways. Origen and Jerome thought it meant the “way of life” of the Jewish people.[10] The term could certainly mean this in the first century (see, e.g., 2 Macc. 4:11; 8:17; 4 Macc. 8:7; 17:9; Josephus, Ant. 15.254), but modern commentators have curiously neglected this option. Instead, they tend to choose one of two other meanings: the special rights that belong to a particular social group (“citizenship”),[11] or a political body (“commonwealth”).[12]

It may be a mistake, however, to distinguish these three meanings too sharply in this passage. That Paul has the privileges of citizenship in mind seems likely from his next phrase, where he expands on the estrangement of his Gentile readers from Israel. They were, he says, ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας (xenoi tōn diathēkōn tēs epangelias, strangers to the covenants of promise),[13] and this is clearly a reference to divine privileges that belonged to those with “citizenship” in Israel. That Paul was thinking of Israel as a discrete people marked out by its own “way of life” also seems likely. As Cohen (1999: 110–19, 125–29) has shown, the term crops up in contexts where the subject is the relationship between the Jewish way of life, embodied in the Mosaic law, and the customs of other peoples (cf. Aletti 2001: 143). Josephus, writing within a few decades of Paul, for example, could use the term to describe what happened when the Jewish high priest Hyrcanus annexed Idumea to Judea in the second century BC. Hyrcanus, he says, “altered their way of life [πολιτεία] and made them adopt the customs and laws of the Jews” (Josephus, Ant. 15.254).[14] Paul is probably also thinking of how unbelieving Gentiles, because they were separated from the people who had access to Israel’s Scriptures and governed their affairs by them (cf. Rom. 3:2; 9:4), were alienated from their “way of life.”[15]

3. Israel’s Scriptures contained not only directions for living as God’s people but also αἱ διαθήκαι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας (hai diathēkai tēs epangelias, the covenants of promise), and Paul’s readers, as Gentiles, were also deprived of the privileges that came with these covenants. What covenants did Paul have in mind? He was probably thinking first of God’s promises to Abraham of descendants and land in Gen. 13:14–16; 15:5, 18; 17:8; and 24:7. The language of covenant occasionally appears in these passages (Gen. 15:18; 17:9–14, 19–21), and Paul explicitly describes God’s promise to Abraham “and to his seed” as a “covenant” in which God gave “promises” (Gal. 3:15–18). The only other covenants Paul mentions in his letters are the Mosaic covenant (Gal. 3:17; 4:24; 2 Cor. 3:14–15) and the new covenant (1 Cor. 11:25; 2 Cor. 3:6; Rom. 11:27). Since Paul sets the promissory character of God’s covenant with Abraham in contrast to the Mosaic covenant (Gal. 3:17–18; 4:23; cf. Heb. 8:6), and since he implies that the Mosaic covenant has passed away (Eph. 2:14–15; cf. Gal. 3:19; 2 Cor. 3:7–11; Rom. 7:6), “the covenants of promise” are probably the covenant with Abraham and the new covenant.[16]

What “promise” do they give? He may simply be thinking generally of the promissory character of the biblical covenants (Lincoln 1990: 137). If Paul (or a disciple steeped in his correspondence) wrote the letter, however, he may well have been thinking more specifically of “the promise of the Spirit” (Gal. 3:14; cf. 2 Cor. 3:6), the promise of the Messiah (cf. Gal. 3:16; Rom. 9:5; and “outside Christ” above), or both.[17] Since Paul has previously said that his readers were sealed with “the promised Holy Spirit” when they received the gospel (1:13), he may have had biblical references to the eschatological gift of the Spirit uppermost in mind (Isa. 32:15; 44:3; Ezek. 11:19; 36:26–27; 37:14; Joel 3:1–2 MT, LXX [2:28–29 Eng.]; cf. Eph. 2:18, 22; Gal. 3:14; Acts 1:4; 2:33; see the comments on Eph. 1:13).

In any case, Israel’s possession of “the covenants of promise” was a significant privilege because these covenants marked out the pathway of God’s saving purposes (cf. Rom. 3:2; 9:4; 2 Tim. 3:15). Gentiles, because of their position outside Israel, had no access to Israel’s Scriptures and therefore no clear access to the saving purposes of God.[18]

4. If Gentiles had no access to Israel’s Scriptures with their promise of blessing (in the Abrahamic covenant) and of a restored relationship between God and his people (in the new covenant), then they also had no hope. The present tense of the participle (ἔχοντες, echontes) implies that outside Israel and before the coming of the gospel to them, Gentiles constantly existed in a state of hopelessness. This does not mean that they felt despair all the time (so, correctly, Best 1998: 242–43), but that from the perspective of a Christian looking back on Gentile existence outside Israel, their future held only “the wrath of God” that “comes upon the sons of disobedience” (5:6; cf. 2:2 and the notes on 1:13).

5. They also were ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ (atheoi en tō kosmō, without God in the world). From their own perspective, many Gentiles would have claimed to be piously devoted to the gods (cf. Jerome [Heine 2002: 133]). The very term Paul uses here, ἄθεος (atheos, without God), was used with disdain by Gentiles to describe the Jews, who refused to worship their gods (Josephus, Ag. Ap. 2.148), and in later times was a favorite slander against Christians for the same reason (Justin, 1 Apol. 6.1; 13.1; 46.3; Athenagoras, Leg. 6.3; Mart. Pol. 3.2).[19] Paul’s perspective here, however, is similar to that of the author of the Martyrdom of Polycarp. The author tells us that when the proconsul commanded the aged bishop to renounce his faith by uttering the anti-Christian slogan “Away with the atheists,” Polycarp turned to the rabble of pagans (ἐθνῶν, ethnōn) gathered to watch him die and, waving his hand toward them, said, “Away with the atheists” (9.2).[20]

Paul has already described existence in “this world” apart from God in 2:1–3. It means living as one of the “sons of disobedience” and therefore under the sway both of this world with its tendency toward evil and of the prince of the demonic realm, the devil himself.

This echo of the terrible plight of those outside of Christ according to 2:1–3 brings to a fitting close Paul’s description of the desperate situation of Gentiles prior to the gospel’s advent. Israel was God’s people and the repository of God’s Word. Prior to the coming of the gospel, only those within the boundaries of Israel had hope for salvation from the wrath that God would pour out on the disobedient. As uncircumcised Gentiles, however, Paul’s readers were by definition excluded from this people and this hope and were therefore in an especially desperate position of hopelessness.

[2:13] The phrase νυνὶ δέ (nuni de, but now) provides the hinge on which the two parts of 2:11–13 swing. Within the NT, the phrase is distinctive of the Pauline Epistles[21] and is used to describe a shift in circumstances (Rom. 15:23, 25; 2 Cor. 8:10–11, 22) or in a line of thought (1 Cor. 12:17–18; 13:12–13; 15:19–20; Rom. 7:15–17). It is not surprising, therefore, that Paul often uses it to mark the dramatic change that accompanies the movement from the period prior to the gospel’s coming to the period of the gospel’s presence (Rom. 3:21), or of the change that comes to people when they move from unbelief to faith (Rom. 6:21–22; 7:5–6; 11:30; Col. 1:21–22; 3:5–8; Philem. 11; cf. Eph. 5:8; 1 Pet. 2:10). Paul used it here to signal that he would now describe the dramatic change that came to his readers thanks to “the surpassing greatness of [God’s] power” (1:19) and despite their desperate plight as Gentiles. Their alienation “once” (v. 11) and “at that time” (v. 12) from the way of life and from the hope described in Israel’s Scriptures had come to an end.

The language Paul uses to describe the Gentiles’ plight and God’s solution to it comes from Isa. 57:19: “Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the LORD; and I will heal them” (NRSV).[22] He will allude more clearly to that text near the end of the next section (2:17), but his use of the adverbs μακράν (makran, far off) and ἐγγύς (engys, near) here is already indebted to it.[23] In its original context, the passage refers to God’s future blessing on Jews wherever they might be, whether scattered abroad or in the land (cf. Acts 2:39), but the wider context from which it comes in Isaiah frequently emphasizes the unification of Israel with all peoples in the worship of God (Isa. 55:5; 56:6–8), and it is easy to see how Paul could have understood it as a prophecy of the inclusion of Gentiles within God’s people through the gospel (Moritz 1996a: 32–34, 45–52).

This eschatological inclusion of Gentiles, as Gentiles, within the people of God has happened ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (en Christō Iēsou, in Christ Jesus) and ἐν τῷ αἵματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ (en tō haimati tou Christou, by the blood of Christ). If the most fundamental problem facing Paul’s Gentile readers prior to the gospel’s arrival among them was their existence “outside Christ” (v. 12), then God has met this problem by placing them “in Christ Jesus.”[24] This could happen, however, only “by his blood,” a notion that Paul has already introduced in 1:7 and that he will explore more fully in the next section (2:14, 16).

Summary

In 2:11–13 Paul begins to describe specifically how God has made his great power available to the church at the corporate level. He does this both by reminding his believing Gentile readers of the plight in which they had existed as people who were separated from Israel and by reminding them of what God has done for them to remedy that plight. He begins by describing the tension-filled divide that existed between Gentiles and Jews prior to the coming of the gospel: both groups considered circumcision an insuperable barrier between them. This social barrier was matched by a theological barrier. As unbelieving Gentiles, Paul’s readers were separated from the Messiah and so from all the blessings of being “in Christ.” They were alienated from Israel’s Scriptures, both from the way of life described there and from the promises the Scriptures contained of a coming Messiah and of the outpouring of God’s Spirit. This meant that they were without hope and without God in a rebellious world headed for the experience of God’s wrath. God responded to this desperate plight, however, by incorporating Paul’s Gentile readers into his people: they are now “in Christ Jesus” and so, although once far from God, have been brought near to him.



Additional Notes

2:11. “Circumcision” (περιτομή) was symbolic to Jews of the social distinction between their people and other peoples, and sometimes in the LXX the designation “uncircumcised” (ἀπερίτμητος) for Gentiles had a pejorative edge.[25] By the first century, Gentiles could simply be called “the foreskin” (ἀκροβυστία; Gal. 2:7; Rom. 3:30; Col. 3:11), and here too the term could be pejorative, as, for example, when m. Ned. 3.11 applies it (in its Hebrew form) to Gentile idolaters.[26]

Gentiles, and especially Romans, however, also considered circumcision to be a distinctive, and negative, characteristic of Jews.[27] The first-century Latin poet Martial, for example, could repeatedly address a Jewish critic of his work as “circumcised poet” (verpe poeta; Epig. 11.94), and he did not intend the description politely (Cohen 1999: 41; cf. Martial, Epig. 7.82; Horace, Sat. 1.9.69–70; Petronius, Satyr. 102; Tacitus, Hist. 5.5; Juvenal, Sat. 14.99, 104).[28] According to Philo, circumcision was “an object of ridicule among many people” (Spec. Laws 1.1). It was so frequently derided in the wider society that many Jews, especially in the first and second centuries AD, sought to have their circumcision disguised by cosmetic surgery (1 Cor. 7:18) or by special mechanisms (Martial, Epig. 7.82).[29]

Although Paul’s primary focus in 2:11–13 is on the Gentiles’ salvation-historical disadvantages when compared to Israel, the way he describes circumcision in 2:11 already hints at the hostility between the two groups, and this will become a dominant theme in 2:14–15 (cf. Col. 3:11; Barth 1974: 254; MacDonald 2000: 241).

2:11. In Greek literature the adjective χειροποίητος frequently means “made by humans” as opposed to “naturally occurring” (LSJ 1985).[30] In the LXX, however, it always appears with negative connotations either to describe “handmade” idols (e.g., Lev. 26:1, 30; Jdt. 8:18; Wis. 14:8; Dan. 5:4, 23; 6:28; Bel 1:5) or, as a substantive, to mean the “idols” themselves (Isa. 2:18; 10:11; 16:12; 19:1; 21:9; 31:7; 46:6). This negative use carries over into the NT where, apart from Eph. 2:11, it always refers to the temple and again has negative connotations: God does not live in a “handmade” temple (Mark 14:58; Acts 7:48), and Christ did not serve as priest in such a temple (Heb. 9:11, 24).[31] This evidence weighs heavily against Yee’s argument (2005: 83–86) that the term is not used in a negative sense in 2:11.﻿[32] Instead, the term probably refers to the merely human surgery by which Jews identifed themselves: physical circumcision is no longer the critical boundary marker for God’s covenant people.





V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)

A. The Special Plight of the Gentiles and God’s Response (2:11–13)

B. Christ Is the Believing Community’s Peace (2:14–18)

C. Gentile Christians as an Integral Part of God’s Household (2:19–22)


B. Christ Is the Believing Community’s Peace (2:14–18)

The next paragraph uses the last phrase of 2:13 as a springboard into an explanation of how and in what senses God in Christ “brought near” those who were “far off.” The section stands out clearly from its context as a discrete unit: it begins with the emphatic pronoun αὐτός (autos, himself) to focus attention on Christ; it shifts from second-person address, used consistently in the previous paragraph (2:11–13) and the following paragraph (2:19–22), to first-person-plural address (apart from 2:17); and in contrast to the surrounding prose, it uses a number of active-voice participles to describe Christ’s action. Christ’s own actions rather than God’s action through Christ, accordingly, take the spotlight in the passage. In addition, the syntax of 2:14–16 is extraordinarily difficult; the passage uses several words that are unique not only to Ephesians but to the entire NT, and it seems to have mingled two independent concepts: the unification of Jews and Gentiles and the reconciliation of humanity with God.

Various explanations have emerged for these unusual aspects of the passage, and three approaches are particularly important. First, some see the paragraph as a Jewish-Christian exegesis of Isa. 9:6–7 (9:5–6 MT, LXX); 52:7; and 57:19. Following normal Jewish midrashic practice, the author has linked these passages together using the catchword “peace” (Stuhlmacher 1986: 187–91; Schnackenburg 1991: 107, 112).

Second, in recent years the idea has emerged that the passage is an encomium (eulogy) on Christ (Faust 1993: 315–24; Aletti 2001: 146; Yee 2005: 136–40). If this is the genre of the passage, Yee argues, then perhaps its parenthetical quality reflects the use of the ancient rhetorical technique of amplification (ἡ αὔξησις, hē auxēsis). This strategy was considered especially appropriate to a speech in praise or blame of someone (an epideictic speech) and that dwelled at length on some unusually noteworthy characteristic or deed of the speech’s subject (Yee 2005: 136–39).[1]

Third, and most popular, is the idea that the letter’s author used a preexisting tradition in this passage, usually thought to be a hymn,[2] and that he modified this tradition to conform to his theological convictions. According to some interpreters, the original hymn pictured Christ breaking through the wall separating heaven from earth in a way reminiscent of Hellenistic Jewish and later gnostic cosmologies (e.g., Schlier 1957: 122–33; cf. Gnilka 1971: 149–50; Lincoln 1990: 128–29; Pokorný 1992: 117–20).[3] The author has modified the hymn to make it refer not merely to the destruction of the barrier between heaven and earth but also to the demolition of the wall of the Mosaic law that separated Jews from Gentiles (v. 15) by the death of Christ on the cross (v. 16; Gnilka 1971: 149, 151; Lincoln 1990: 128; Pokorný 1992: 118–19).

What are we to make of these explanations for the parenthetical nature and complicated syntax of 2:14–18? As for the first two ideas, there is perhaps no way to know the extent to which Jewish midrashic or Greco-Roman rhetorical practice influenced the author. It seems reasonable to think that one or the other or both at the same time had some impact on the way Paul expresses himself here. This is all the more plausible if we think of the author as a highly educated Hellenistic Jew (like Paul). Whether any such influence is present, and the extent to which it is present, however, is so uncertain that it seems unwise to allow it to control the exegesis of the passage.

Although the third explanation has enjoyed immense influence, it must receive the same verdict. The focus on Christ, the unusual vocabulary, the difficult syntax, and the shift of attention from peace between Jews and Gentiles to reconciliation with God might be explained by reliance on traditional material. But is the case certain enough to form a solid basis for exegesis? Ephesians, after all, is a syntactically difficult text (see, e.g., 1:13; 2:4–6; 3:1–2, 14; 4:20), and nearly 10 percent of its vocabulary is unique within the NT, about the same percentage as in 2:14–18 (Best 1997a: 61; 1998: 249). If we remember Jesus’s own formulation of the two great commandments, moreover, the reconciliation of human beings to one another and of human beings generally to God seem to be natural thematic partners in a Christian text (Mark 12:28–31; Matt. 22:35–40; Luke 10:25–28; Did. 1.2; Justin, Dial. 93). More detailed interaction with those who advocate an underlying hymn must await the exegesis of the passage, but enough has been said to show that the theory is too uncertain to contribute to a reliable interpretive strategy.[4]

Rhetorically, Eph. 2:14–18 functions in a way not unlike other Pauline excurses. In 1 Cor. 12:1–13:13 a discussion of the need to value all spiritual gifts to avoid division in the church body (12:1–31) leads to an excursus on the importance of love (13:1–13). In 2 Cor. 2:14–7:1, a narrative of Paul’s difficult relationship with the Corinthians leads to a lengthy reflection on the nature of his apostolic ministry.

Although briefer, Eph. 2:14–18 is also an excursus. It is intended to show how Christ brought Gentiles, who were “far” from the salvation-historical privileges of Israel, “near” both to Jews, from whom they were alienated, and to God. By his death on the cross, Christ tore down and set aside the Mosaic law. It had formed a wall of hostility that divided Jews from Gentiles and, as Paul’s use of the term “access” (προσαγωγή, prosagōgē) in 2:18 hints, blocked the way between humanity and God. Paul seems to assume that the Mosaic law’s “decrees” (δόγματα, dogmata, v. 15) separating Israel and the nations led to enmity between the two groups. He also seems to assume that these “decrees” have codified the enmity between all humanity and God (cf. 2:1–3; cf. Col. 2:14–15). When Christ died on the cross, he tore down (λύσας, lysas; Eph. 2:14) the Mosaic law by setting it aside (καταργήσας, katargēsas; v. 15) along with its powerful effects on sinful humanity. Here Paul probably assumes the theology of the Mosaic law that he has developed in Romans. Through no fault of its own, the Mosaic law’s introduction increased the trespass and only made rebellion against God worse (Rom. 5:20; 7:11–12). With its removal, the way was clear for the union of Jewish and Gentile believers in Christ (Eph. 2:15) and the Spirit (v. 16), and for the reconciliation between all humanity, across ethnic lines, to God (vv. 16–18). The first phrase of the passage aptly summarizes all this: “He himself is our peace.”



Exegesis and Exposition

14For he himself is our peace, who made both things one and tore down in his flesh the middle wall, that is, the fence—the enmity—15aby setting aside the law of commandments [promulgated] in [the form of] decrees, 15bin order that he might create the two into one new human being in him, so making peace, 16and might reconcile both, in one body, to God through the cross by killing the enmity in it. 17And he came and preached peace to you who were far and peace to those who were near, 18for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

[2:14–15a] The γάρ (gar, for) connects the new paragraph firmly with the immediately preceding statement that the Gentiles, who were “far,” have now “been brought near” both “in Christ Jesus” and “by the blood of Christ.” Although it is true, as advocates of an underlying hymn claim, that Christ now becomes the subject of the action whereas before in Ephesians God has been the subject and Christ the agent through whom God works, 2:13 has already prepared the ground for Christ to take center stage.[5] Paul intends to show precisely how Christ’s death overcame the estrangement of Gentiles from the people of God that he has portrayed in 2:11–12. The αὐτός (autos, he himself) places the spotlight directly on Christ (cf. 4:10–11; 5:23; 5:27).

Christ, Paul says, ἐστὶν ἡ εἰρήνη ἡμῶν (estin hē eirēnē hēmōn, is our peace). The identification of Christ with “our peace” is striking and is probably derived from the idea that those who are “in Christ” (v. 13) assume some of the qualities of Christ himself (cf. 5:2; 1 Cor. 1:30; Col. 3:3–4). Christ is not divided into competing groups, and so those who are identified with Christ are also at peace with one another (1 Cor. 1:13; 12:12–13, 27; Rom. 12:5).[6] As many commentators observe, the “peace” Paul thinks of here is the broad Hebraic concept of שָׁלוֹם (šālôm, peace), which does not mean simply the cessation of hostilities.[7] The word certainly can also mean the “opposite of war” (HALOT 2:1508), however, and in light of Paul’s emphasis on the alienation of Gentiles from Israel (2:11–12), this nuance is probably uppermost in his thinking here.

With three participial clauses, Paul next explains how Christ has produced peace between the two formerly alienated social groups. First, Christ is ὁ ποιήσας τὰ ἀμφότερα ἕν (ho poiēsas ta amphotera hen, he who made both things one). It is odd that Paul uses the neuter form of the adjective ἀμφότεροι (amphoteroi, both) and the number ἕν (hen, one) here since he has used masculine terms to refer to Jews and Gentiles in 2:11–13,﻿[8] and the two other occurrences of ἀμφότεροι in 2:16 and 18 are both masculine. This has led some interpreters to see the neuter terms here as undigested bits of traditional material that originally referred to a division between the heavenly and the earthly spheres rather than to two groups of people (e.g., Schlier 1957: 124; Gnilka 1971: 139; Lindemann 1975: 157n66, 160; Lincoln 1990: 140). If this is right, however, it is difficult to know why Paul did not change the neuter forms to masculines as he did in 2:16 and 18 (Best 1998: 252). Best’s alternative suggestion is attractive: since the reference to a wall in what follows calls on spatial imagery, the author may have already been thinking in those terms and thus of a Jewish “region” and a Gentile “region,” which the wall separates. In Greek, the noun “region” (χωρίον, chōrion) is neuter, and so it could serve as the unexpressed antecedent of the neuter ἀμφότερα and ἕν.[9]

Second, Paul describes Christ as ὁ . . . τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ λύσας (ho . . . to mesotoichon tou phragmou lysas, he who tore down the middle wall, that is the fence).[10] The term μεσότοιχον is rare in Greek literature, but where it does occur, it refers either to an outside wall or to a partition wall in a house or temple.[11] Josephus could use the closely related phrase τὸν μέσον τοῖχον (ton meson toichon, the middle wall) to refer to the wall that separated the holy of holies from the rest of Solomon’s temple (Ant. 8.71; cf. 1 Kings 6:16–17; BDAG 635). Paul is using μεσότοιχον here metaphorically of something that keeps the two people groups, Jews and Gentiles, separate from each other. He further defines τὸ μεσότοιχον with the explanatory (or “epexegetical”) genitive τοῦ φραγμοῦ (tou phragmou). This term means a “fence” or “hedge” that encloses something, shutting it off and protecting it (e.g., Isa. 5:2, 5; Sir. 36:25; Mark 12:1; Matt. 21:33), and appears only here in the Pauline corpus. Christ, then, tore down a partition that was also an enclosing fence (Eadie 1883: 172).

Why did Paul express himself in such an unusual way, using two rare terms in a redundant construction? According to Josephus, Herod’s temple had a short stone wall or “balustrade” (δρύφακτος, dryphaktos) that separated the outer area, to which Gentiles were permitted, from the inner, more-holy sections permitted only to Jews (Ant. 15.417; J.W. 5.193–95).[12] The idea that Paul refers to this wall here as a metaphor for the separation of Jews and Gentiles is very old, going back at least to Anselm of Laon in the early twelfth century (Eadie 1883: 172), and has had a steady stream of supporters to the present (e.g., Abbott 1897: 61; Robinson 1904: 59–60; MacDonald 2000: 244; cf. MacDonald 2004: 434).[13] On this reading, Paul refers to this enclosure with the entire phrase τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ and uses it as a symbol of the hostility between Jews and Gentiles. It is unlikely, however, that Paul would have expected a wide audience of Gentiles in Asia Minor to understand an allusive reference to a specific feature of the Jerusalem temple’s exterior architecture.[14]

Others have argued that the term μεσότοιχον, before the author glossed it with τοῦ φραγμοῦ, came from a piece of tradition, perhaps a hymn, in which it referred to the separation of earth from heaven according to a Hellenistic Jewish, and later gnostic, cosmology. The author added the reference to the enclosing “fence” because that term was particularly appropriate to the Mosaic law’s function of protecting Israel from the impurities and idolatries of the Gentiles. The author, then, has transformed a hymn that originally spoke of Christ overcoming the separation between heaven and earth (cf. Col. 1:20) into a statement of Christ’s destruction of the Mosaic law (e.g., Gnilka 1971: 151; Lincoln 1990: 129, 141; Pokorný 1992: 121).

This interpretation falls prey to the objections already voiced against the theory that 2:14–18, or some part of it, consists of a traditional hymn and Paul’s (or the author’s) editing of it. In this instance, it is difficult to see why, if the term μεσότοιχον seemed inadequate to Paul, he did not simply replace it with φραγμός rather than adding φραγμός to it.

Others believe that the wall simply symbolizes social separation and has no very specific reference. Jews were separated from Gentiles by a host of social boundaries, and so the metaphor of a wall, without particular reference to any specific institution, is used to describe the distance and sometimes hostility between Jews and Gentiles (Best 1998: 256–57; Yee 2005: 151).

We should not exaggerate the strangeness of Judaism, however, relative to the rest of Greco-Roman society in the first century. In a careful study of the issue, Cohen (1999: 28), concludes, “Not a single ancient author says that Jews are distinctive because of their looks, clothing, speech, names, or occupations.” According to Cohen (1999: 67) “The diaspora Jews of antiquity were not easily recognizable—if, indeed, they were recognizable at all.”

The most reliable social indicator that someone was a Jew, although itself far from infallible, was observance of the Jewish law (Cohen 1999: 53–62).[15] In 49–48 BC, about a century before Paul wrote Ephesians, the Roman proconsul of Asia, Lucius Lentulus Crus, exempted Jews in Ephesus who were also Roman citizens from military service. The Jews of Ephesus were distinguished from everybody else because they “observed” and “practiced” Jewish rites (ἱερὰ Ἰουδαϊκά, hiera Ioudaika); in other words, they kept the Jewish law (Cohen 1999: 58; Josephus, Ant. 14.228, 234, 237, 240). Since we know that in the Jewish Diaspora of the Second Temple period, the law was compared to “iron walls” (σιδηρᾶ τείχη, sidēra teichē) that God used to “enclose” Israel “with a fence” (περιφράσσω, periphrassō) and so to keep them from mixing with “other nations” (ἄλλα ἔθνη, alla ethnē; Let.
