Arist. 139),[16] and since we know that observing the law was the main distinguishing characteristic of Ephesian Jews during the same period, it seems most likely that by the phrase τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ Paul meant the Jewish law. The Jewish law was both a “partition” that separated Jews from Gentiles and a “fence” that enclosed the Jewish people, keeping them safe from Gentile influences.

The next two phrases pose major syntactical problems. It is unclear whether τὴν ἔχθραν (tēn echthran, the enmity) is the direct object of the second participle, λύσας (lysas, who tore down), or of the third participle, καταργήσας (katargēsas, having set aside). If it goes with λύσας, then, somewhat oddly, the two objects of that participle, each standing in apposition to the other, appear on either side of their verb rather than one after the other (Lincoln 1990: 124). If τὴν ἔχθραν goes with καταργήσας and stands in apposition to τὸν νόμον (ton nomon, the law), however, then the phrase ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ (en tē sarki autou, in his flesh) intervenes between the two objects of the verb although it modifies neither of them (Abbott 1897: 62; Hoehner 2002: 373). It is difficult to decide between these alternatives, and precisely this kind of syntactical problem has led many students of the letter to conclude that Paul modified an underlying text of some kind (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 124).

Syntactical problems are not unusual in Ephesians, however, and may be the result of the letter’s oral quality.[17] When Paul dictated the letter, he paused either after saying “λύσας” or after saying “τὴν ἔχθραν,” making clear where τὴν ἔχθραν should go in the flow of thought. Since we do not know where that oral pause occurred, we are reduced to making an educated guess, and so it seems slightly more likely that τὴν ἔχθραν goes with λύσας. It is closer to it and could have come into the sentence as something of an afterthought (cf. χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι in 2:5). Christ, then, is the one who has torn down “the middle wall, that is, the fence—the enmity.”

The next phrase, ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ, also poses problems. It can fall, conceptually, in three different places. The following list illustrates this with three English translations that place the words “in his flesh” in italic type and the word(s) the phrase modifies in bold type:



It could modify ὁ . . . λύσας: “he who tore down in his flesh the middle wall, that is the fence—the enmity.”[18]

It might modify καταργήσας: “he who tore down the middle wall, that is the fence—the enmity, by setting aside in his flesh the law of commandments in ordinances.”[19]

It might also be an afterthought intended to show that Christ was the central figure who accomplished the action of all three participles: “who made (ποιήσας) the two one, having torn down (λύσας) the middle wall, that is the fence—the enmity (in his flesh), by setting aside (καταργήσας) the law of commandments in ordinances” (Best 1998: 234, 258).

Probably the first of these options is correct (the middle wall was torn down in Christ’s flesh). Many commentators whose native tongue was ancient Greek have favored it (e.g., Origen [Heine 2002: 135]; Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.40]; Oecumenius, PG 118:1197), and the appearance of the phrase τὴν ἔχθραν ἐν αὐτῷ in 2:16 hints that the prepositional phrase “in his flesh” should stay with τὴν ἔχθραν.

What does the phrase mean? The similarity of the phrase to 2:13, 16 and Col. 1:22 (cf. Col. 2:14), where Christ’s death is the means of reconciliation between God and human beings (v. 16; Col. 1:22; 2:14) and between Jews and Gentiles (Eph. 2:13), means that it must refer to Jesus’s death on the cross, not to his incarnation (pace Calvin 1965: 151). Paul probably did not intend to emphasize Christ’s identity with “sinful flesh” (pace Muddiman 2001: 130, citing Rom. 8:3) but only that his death was a physical sacrifice, involving “blood” (Eph. 2:13; cf. 1:7) and “flesh.”

The third participial phrase modifies the second participle λύσας, explaining the means by which Christ tore down the dividing wall that was also the enmity between Jews and Gentiles (Wallace 1996: 628–30). He did this “by setting aside” (καταργήσας, katargēsas) the law. Paul uses this same verb in the passive voice in 2 Cor. 3:7–14 to say that the Mosaic era, with its “ministry of death, chiseled in letters on stone tablets,” has been “set aside” (2 Cor. 3:7 NRSV; cf. 3:11, 13–14). He also uses it in the passive voice in Rom. 7:2 and 6 to speak of believers being “released” from the law just as a wife is released, when her husband dies, from the law binding her to him. That is the sense Paul intends here, although by putting the verb in the active voice, and using it in concert with the terms “tore down” (v. 14) and “kill” (v. 16), he gives it a somewhat stronger connotation.[20]

If the passage says in strong terms that Christ set aside the law, however, does this not put it in tension with the Paul of the undisputed letters? In Rom. 3:31 Paul insists that his gospel does not set aside the law (using καταργέω in the active voice), and he continues to use the law for ethical instruction in such places as Gal. 5:14; 1 Cor. 5:13; 9:8–9; 10:1–22; 14:33b–34; and Rom. 13:8–10.

Some interpreters have thought that a contradiction does exist and is attributable to the context out of which the supposedly post-Pauline author of Ephesians wrote. He lived at a time when the Jewish law was seen as equivalent to the Jewish way of life, which separated Jews from Gentiles and so, for Christians, could be safely relegated to the irrelevance of past salvation history. The intense discussions that once took place between Paul and Jewish Christianity were now a distant memory. There was no longer a need for Paul’s more nuanced approach to the Mosaic law, in which it was in some senses abrogated and in other senses established. The redundant phrase used to describe the law in 2:15 (ὁ νόμος τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν, ho nomos tōn entolōn en dogmasin, the law of commandments in ordinances) only emphasizes the completeness of the law’s abrogation—Christ did away with every facet of the Jewish way of life (Lincoln 1987: 612, 616; 1990: 143; Schnackenburg 1991: 115; MacDonald 2000: 245).

Other interpreters have moved in precisely the opposite direction, understanding 2:15 to set aside only certain elements of the Mosaic law. Calvin, followed by a number of others over the years, believed that the phrase τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν limited the part of the law under discussion to its “ceremonies”—those particularly Jewish parts of the law that formed the “wall” of the previous verse and separated Jews from Gentiles. The moral law, common to both Jews and Gentiles, then remained unaffected by Christ’s work (Calvin: 1965: 151; 1973: 196).[21] Others have thought that the phrase sets aside only the commanding character of the law, with its emphasis on externals and obedience (Robinson 1904: 64, 161; Muddiman 2001: 133).

None of these interpretations of the expression ὁ νόμος τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν καταργήσας, however, is satisfactory. The words τῶν ἐντολῶν express the content of the law, and the phrase ἐν δόγμασιν describes the method of the commandments’ promulgation.[22] The law that Christ set aside consisted of specific commandments promulgated in the form of decrees.[23] The redundancy of the expression is characteristic of Ephesians, and so we should probably not read too much significance into each word. Paul clearly intends the phrase to refer to the entire Mosaic law.[24]

The Paul of Ephesians did not think that Christ had set aside the need for “commandments” within Christianity, nor did he think the Mosaic law had been “nullified,” if that word is taken to mean that the Mosaic law is no longer useful for believers. His use of a “command” (ἐντολή, entolē) from the Decalogue in his ethical instruction in Ephesians (6:2–3; cf. Exod. 20:12; Deut. 5:16) is enough to demonstrate this. Paul apparently thought, however, that when believers obeyed the parts of the Mosaic law that he incorporated into his ethical teaching, they were not obeying these commands as the Mosaic law. In Paul’s thinking, the Mosaic law governed Israel for a specific period of time (Gal. 3:19). Although it was glorious in its day (2 Cor. 3:7–10), it had now served its purpose and come to its divinely appointed end (2 Cor. 3:13; Rom. 10:4). God had established a new people, comprised of both Jews and Gentiles, and the law governing their conduct Paul called “the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2; cf.1 Cor. 9:21). The Mosaic law was still authoritative Scripture within the new people of God, but in a different way than it had been for Israel.[25] It revealed the character of God, the nature of humanity, and the centrality of faith to a right relationship with God, but its commandments no longer governed the behavior of God’s people without first passing through the filter of the gospel.

Here, then, Paul says that when Christ set aside the Mosaic law by his death, he removed the hostile purposes to which human sinfulness had often put the Mosaic law’s good, but temporary, commands about separating from the Gentiles. This toxic mixture of the law and human sinfulness (cf. Rom. 5:20; 7:5, 7–25; 1 Cor. 15:56) probably led Paul to speak of the law here in 2:15 in negative terms. The sinful use of the law produced a hostility that deprived Gentiles of access to God through the Scriptures (2:12). There is certainly more to be said about the Mosaic law than this, but a fuller explanation of its role did not fit Paul’s purposes here. Instead, he speaks concisely, aligning the Mosaic law closely with “enmity” and saying in straightforward terms that Christ has set it aside (Aletti 2001: 151).

[2:15b–16] Christ set aside the Mosaic law for two purposes. Paul now describes these purposes in a lengthy subordinate clause with two main verbs, κτίσῃ (ktisē, he might create) and ἀποκαταλλάξῃ (apokatallaxē, he might reconcile).

First, when Christ set aside the Mosaic law, he created a new, unified human being in himself and so made peace between believers from among Jews and Gentiles. Paul has already used the verb κτίζω (ktizō, create) to refer to the individual believer as God’s new creation no longer living under the sway of the world, the devil, and the flesh but in the way God originally created human beings to live (2:10; cf. vv. 2–3).[26] Here too Paul has the new creation in mind, but now conceived as a corporate event, making peace between the two estranged groups, Jews and Gentiles.[27] In bringing these groups together, Christ has created εἷς καινὸς ἄνθρωπος (heis kainos anthrōpos, one new human being), and he has done this ἐν αὐτῷ (en autō, in him[self]). By their union with Christ, believers become united with one another across the social barriers that formerly divided them, and so, like Christ himself, become a new Adam (cf. 1 Cor. 15:22, 45–49; Col. 3:10–11; Lincoln 1990: 143). Ποιῶν (poiōn; v. 15) is a textbook example of an adverbial participle of result: it is in the present tense and follows the verb (Wallace 1996: 637–39). So the result of this newly created man, Paul says, is peace between formerly hostile Jews and Gentiles.

Second, when Christ set aside the Mosaic law, he reconciled all humanity, of whatever ethnic origin, to God. “Reconciliation” between God and human beings is a distinctively Pauline concept within the NT and appears in two theologically weighty passages in the undisputed letters: 2 Cor. 5:18–20 and Rom. 5:10–11 (cf. Rom. 11:15). In these passages, God always takes the initiative in reconciliation, although he does so through Christ, and specifically through his death. This does not mean that people have no responsibility in reconciliation, however, for God gives to Paul a ministry of reconciliation, and that ministry involves calling people to “be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5:20 NRSV; on this point, see Büchsel, TDNT 1:256–57). Just as with the everyday use of “reconciliation” (1 Cor. 7:11), the theological use of the term assumes a breech in relationship, an enmity (Rom. 5:1, 8, 10), which needs to be healed. In the undisputed letters, this enmity originates in human rebellion against God, and this rebellion has called forth God’s wrath (Rom. 1:18–3:19; 5:9; see Büchsel, TDNT 1:257).

The concept in Colossians (1:20, 22) and Ephesians (only here in 2:16) is basically the same but with three distinctions. First, both letters use the unique compounded verb ἀποκαταλλάσσω (apokatallassō) rather than the usual terms καταλλάσσω (katallassō, reconcile) and καταλλαγή (katallagē, reconciliation). This variation probably only intensifies the word rather than changing its meaning.[28] Second, in both letters reconciliation comes through Christ’s death, but Christ, rather than God himself, is the reconciler. Third, whereas in the undisputed letters and Ephesians, God reconciles people to himself, in Colossians he reconciles the entire cosmos (τὰ πάντα, ta panta, all things) to himself (1:20).

Here in 2:16, Paul says that Christ has reconciled τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους (tous amphoterous, both) to God, using the masculine adjective, whereas in 2:14 he had used the neuter τά ἀμφότερα. The change is slightly unusual, and some interpreters believe that it signals Paul’s (or the author’s) editorial work on an original hymn that once referred not to two groups of people but to two cosmic spheres, heaven and earth (see above on v. 14). A simpler explanation, however, is ready to hand. Since the appearance of τά ἀμφότερα in 2:14, Paul has introduced the grammatically masculine expression καινὸς ἄνθρωπος (kainos anthrōpos, new human being) in 2:15b, and since this new human being is made of “both” Jews and Gentiles, Paul has shifted the adjective “both” into the masculine gender to fit the personal and grammatically masculine nature of the metaphor (so also Mayer 2002: 131). As 2:1–3 has clarified, all people are “sons of disobedience” and “children of wrath.” Thus, although the Jewish advantages Paul has described in 2:12 mean that Jews were in some sense “nearer” to God than Gentiles were (cf. v. 17), they were still in need of reconciliation to him through the death of Christ.

They are reconciled to him ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι (en heni sōmati, in one body). As the use of εἷς (heis, one) shows, Paul refers here not to the crucified body of Christ[29] but to the “one entity [ἕν, hen]” (v. 14) and the “one [εἷς] new human being” (v. 15) formed of Jews and Gentiles who are “in Christ.” The body to which Paul refers therefore is the church, a body of people unified with each other across ethnic lines and at peace with God (cf. Col. 3:15).

Paul next describes the specific means through which this reconciliation with God was able to take place. It happened διὰ τοῦ σταυροῦ (dia tou staurou, through the cross), that is, by means of Christ’s death on the cross. Even more specifically, it happened ἀποκτείνας τὴν ἔχθραν (apokteinas tēn echthran, by killing the enmity).[30] Paul last used the term ἔχθρα (echthra, enmity) of the social tension between Jews and Gentiles that Christ “tore down in his flesh” (v. 14), and some commentators continue to read ἔχθρα here in those terms: Christ’s death on the cross killed the enmity between Jews and Gentiles (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 146; Best 1998: 266). But between his use of ἔχθρα in 2:14 and his use of it here, Paul has introduced the theme of the reconciliation of all humanity to God, and this theme will dominate the rest of the paragraph (cf. vv. 17–18). The term here, then, refers to the enmity between God and his rebellious creatures, and the whole thought is reminiscent of Rom. 5:10: “For if, while we were enemies [ἐχθροί, echthroi] we were reconciled [κατηλλάγημεν, katēllagēmen] to God through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled [καταλλαγέντες, katallagentes], shall we be saved by his life” (cf., e.g., O’Brien 1999: 204–5; Hoehner 2002: 283–84).

Since ἀποκτείνας τὴν ἔχθραν serves to further specify precisely how Christ used the cross to reconcile both Jews and Gentiles to God, the prepositional phrase ἐν αὐτῷ (en autō, in it) probably also refers to the cross (e.g., Gnilka 1973: 144–45; Best 1998: 266; Hoehner 2002: 384) rather than to Christ himself (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 146; Schnackenburg 1991: 117). The killing of the enmity happened when Christ was killed on the cross. This thought not only recalls the reference to the death of God’s Son in Rom. 5:10 but, since it is part of a statement about Christ’s purpose in setting aside the Mosaic law, the expression is also reminiscent of Col. 2:14–15: “[Christ] erased the record of debts, with its decrees [δόγμασιν, dogmasin], which was against us, and removed it from the midst, nailing it to the cross. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by it [ἐν αὐτῷ, en autō].”

The Mosaic law was as tightly bound to the enmity between God and all humanity as it was to the enmity between Jews and Gentiles. When its holy, righteous, and good “decrees” encountered a humanity under the power of the world, the devil, and the flesh, they served only to reveal the depth of humanity’s rebellion against God and the gravity of the penalty for that rebellion. When Christ died on the cross, he set the law aside, and in so doing, he not only created a new people unified across ethnic barriers but also removed the case against all humanity codified in the Mosaic law. When Christ set aside the law through his death on the cross, therefore, he reconciled to God all who believed the gospel, whether Jew or Gentile.

[2:17] Paul now summarizes the dual theme of peace between Jews and Gentiles and peace between humanity and God with a skillfully crafted allusion to Isa. 52:7a and 57:19. Isaiah 52:7a refers to the beauty of “the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news” (NRSV).[31] In Isaiah, this good news is God’s restoration of Israel’s fortunes after the exile and, with it, the eschatological reign of God. Paul was apparently not the first early Christian to connect this text with the realization that in Christ, God was restoring peace between himself and not only Israel but also all humanity. For Peter too, in Acts 10:36 (cf. Luke 2:14), Christ is the messenger of Isa. 52:7, who proclaims to Israel the glad tidings (εὐαγγελίζω, euangelizō) of peace and who is also, as Peter puts it, “Lord of all” (cf. Faust 1993: 159).

As he has already hinted in 2:13, however, Paul’s primary concern is not with Isa. 52:7 but with Isa. 57:19. Paul now weaves an allusion to this text into his argument by repeating the term “peace” and so recalling the statement “peace, peace, to the far and the near” (NRSV).[32] He cleverly restructures the statement in Isaiah so that one occurrence of the word “peace” goes with “far” and another with “near” (Lincoln 1982: 28; 1990: 149). This restructuring emphasizes the evenhandedness of the proclamation of the glad tidings: the Gentiles have received the message of peace just as decisively as God’s own people. Their greater distance from God has made no difference. The “peace,” then, is not a peace between Jews and Gentiles (as it was in vv. 14 and 15) but a peace between both groups and God.[33]

[2:18] Paul now provides further evidence of the peace that both Jews and Gentiles who are in Christ have with God. Both have been reconciled to God, “for” (ὅτι, hoti) both groups are united in the Spirit and have access to the Father through Christ.

The ὅτι introduces neither the result of Christ’s proclamation of peace (Hoehner 2002: 218) nor the content of the proclamation (Haupt 1902a: 88), but loosely indicates the basis for, or proof of, the peace that Christ has proclaimed (LSJ 1265; BDAG 732.4b).[34] This proof comes in the form of ἡ προσαγωγή (he prosagōgē, the access) that Christ has provided to God for both Jews and Gentiles. Προσαγωγή could refer to access to a king, and some distinguished interpreters have taken it that way here (LSJ 1500; Fee 1994: 685): just as the friends of Cyrus could introduce members of the common people to Cyrus and gain them an audience with the great king (Xenophon, Cyr. 7.5.45), so Christ leads us into the presence of God.

In this passage, however, God is depicted not as a king but as a Father. It seems more likely, then, that when Paul uses προσαγωγή here, he has in mind the common meaning of its cognate verb προσάγω, which often refers to bringing offerings, prayers, or people before God (Gärtner 1965: 60–62; Lincoln 1990: 149).[35] As we have just seen in the comments on 2:15–16, Paul has implied that the Mosaic law was a barrier not only between Jews and Gentiles (v. 14) but also between God and humanity (v. 16). Through his death on the cross (διὰ τοῦ σταυροῦ, dia tou staurou, through the cross), Christ removed this barrier (v. 16) and so provided access to God (cf. Rom. 4:15; 5:1–2, 9–10). Paul’s phrase δι’ αὐτοῦ (di’ autou, through him; v. 18) probably refers precisely to Christ’s death as the means through which he has obtained access to God for all who believe the gospel proclamation of peace.[36] Through his own death, Christ has brought people into God’s presence just as a priest might bring an offering to a deity.

Paul identifies the group who is now at peace with God as οἱ ἀμφότεροι (hoi amphoteroi), “both” Jews and Gentiles.[37] They come to God ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι (en heni pneumati), meaning not “by means of one Spirit” but “united together in one Spirit.” Two considerations make this second understanding of the phrase clear. First, Paul has already mentioned the means of access to God: it is provided by Christ’s death. Second, thus far he has used the number “one” twice within this paragraph to speak of the unity of Jews and Gentiles in Christ, in the phrase “one new human being” in 2:15 and in the phrase “in one body” in 2:16. Here too, then, his focus is on the unity of Jews and Gentiles. They are one just as the Spirit is one, and in this Spirit-effected unity they come to God, an approach made possible by the death of Christ (cf. 4:3–4 and the comments of Fee 1994: 583–84).

Summary

In 2:14–18 Paul places the spotlight directly on Christ, who, he says, is the “peace” of the believing community. He is their peace in the sense that he has united Jews and Gentiles to each other in himself and therefore overcome the hostility vividly portrayed in 2:11–12. Paul’s description of how Christ did this moves forward in three steps. These steps are not related to one another sequentially but examine the same action in increasing detail, like a microscope clicking through three levels of magnification to examine the same organism:

Christ made the two groups one.

Christ tore down the Mosaic law as both a “partition” separating Jews from Gentiles and as a “fence” enclosing the Jewish people and keeping them safe from Gentile influences.

Christ tore down this “partition” between Jews and Gentiles by setting aside the Mosaic law’s commandments, issued in the form of decrees. When the Mosaic law passed away, its use as an instrument of hostility between Jews and Gentiles also passed away.

Christ set aside the Mosaic law for two reasons. First, he did this to create in himself one new human being out of two formerly hostile factions. Paul’s description of this purpose summarizes all that he has just said. The second purpose, in contrast, introduces a new thought: when Christ set aside the law, he reconciled this unified group of Jewish and Gentile believers to God.

Christ did all this, Paul says, through his death on the cross. His death made it possible for him to present to God both Jewish and Gentile believers, now united peacefully with each other as a newly created human being.





V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)

A. The Special Plight of the Gentiles and God’s Response (2:11–13)

B. Christ Is the Believing Community’s Peace (2:14–18)

C. Gentile Christians as an Integral Part of God’s Household (2:19–22)


C. Gentile Christians as an Integral Part of God’s Household (2:19–22)

After making the case that, in Christ Jesus, Gentile Christians have drawn near both to Jewish Christians and to God (2:13, 17–18), Paul next shows exactly how near all Christians are to one another and to God. Using as a starting point his concluding statement that both Jewish Christians and Gentile Christians now have access “to the Father,” he explains that Gentile Christians are full members of God’s household (v. 19). This in turn leads him to employ the architectural metaphor of a building under construction to describe the close relationship his Gentile Christian readers have to their Jewish fellow Christians and to God himself (v. 20).

They became members of God’s household when God constructed them on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, a foundation whose most important stone—the stone that gives guidance to the building process and stability to the finished structure—is Christ Jesus himself. In the sphere marked out by a relationship with him, Paul continues, this whole building is presently growing into a temple whose individual building blocks are tightly fitted together (v. 21). Paul is probably thinking especially of the close connection that now exists between his Gentile Christian readers (v. 22) and Jewish Christians since Christ has set aside the Mosaic law. He then turns directly to his Gentile Christian readers and tells them that they too are being built into this structure together with others, presumably the Jewish Christians to whom peace was preached, according to 2:17. The entire building, he concludes, is the place where God dwells by his Spirit.

This paragraph reexpresses the main themes of 2:11–18 in vivid metaphorical language and brings all of 2:1–22 to a fitting and emphatic end. Paul has demonstrated to his Gentile Christian readers the depth of their plight prior to their trust in the gospel at both the individual and corporate levels. Individually, God has rescued them from being led toward his eschatological wrath by the world, its evil prince, and their own sinful tendencies (2:1–3). Corporately, God rescued them from an ethnic hostility that kept them alienated from both the promises of God in the Scriptures and from God himself. In 2:19–22, with the metaphor of the construction of God’s dwelling place, Paul summarizes for his readers precisely what God’s powerful action on their behalf (1:19) has done for them.

Through the apostolic and prophetic preaching of the gospel, God has placed them in his household. He has fitted them into his house alongside Jewish believers, overcoming the alienation that previously existed between Jews and Gentiles. He has also placed them in the very house where he dwells by his Spirit, overcoming their estrangement from him.

God has accomplished all this “in” Christ Jesus. As the building’s most important stone, Christ Jesus guides the building process, stabilizes the building itself, and presides over it from his position of authority in the heavenly places, where he reigns. Through him the alienation of Gentiles from Jews and of both groups from God has been so fully overcome that both groups fit tightly together to form the place where God’s Spirit dwells.

Paul’s statement in 2:18, which seems to form a launching pad for the present paragraph, provides a neat summary of these points: “Through him [Christ] we both [Gentiles and Jews] have access in one Spirit to the Father.”



Exegesis and Exposition

19So then, you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens together with the saints and members of God’s household 20because you were built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the most important stone, 21in whom the whole ⌜ ⌝ building, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, 22in whom also you are being built together into the dwelling place of God in the Spirit.

[2:19] Ἄρα οὖν (ara oun, so then) is characteristic of Paul’s argumentative style, and here it signals a tight logical connection between 2:18 and the statement that Paul is about to make.[1] Since access to the Father has been achieved through the death of Christ for a group united in the Spirit across ethnic lines, and since Paul’s Gentile readers belong to this group (v. 18), they are neither “strangers” (ξένοι, xenoi) nor “aliens” (πάροικοι, paroikoi) but “citizens together” (συμπολῖται, sympolitai) and “members of the household” (οἰκεῖοι) of God.

These four terms were commonly used in social and political contexts to refer to a particular group’s status, and ξένοι and πάροικοι were frequently contrasted with πολῖται or οἰκεῖοι. Ancient lists of city residents, for example, ranked the privileges of full citizens (πολῖται) first, resident aliens (πάροικοι or κάτοικοι, katoikoi) next, and transient foreigners (ξένοι) last.[2] Philo (Posterity 109), similarly, describes how people adopt a different form of speech depending on the social status of the person to whom they are speaking: one speaks in a different way to parents than to children, to near relatives than to distant ones, to members of one’s own household (οἰκείοις, oikeiois) than to foreigners (ἀλλοτρίοις, allotriois), and to citizens (πολίταις, politais) than to strangers (ξένοις, xenois).[3]

“Strangers” and “aliens,” therefore, were outsiders without the full legal rights of citizens and often, at a more informal level, without social acceptance from the communities in which they lived. Paul uses the terms metaphorically and loosely. He neither intends to make technical distinctions between ξένοι and πάροικοι (pace Eadie 1883: 189) nor is interested in the legal nicety that these groups were not entirely without rights, especially in Jewish society (J. H. Elliott 1981: 25, 27–28). Instead, he paints in broad brush strokes, intending to contrast the former status of his Gentile readers as outside the people of God, with their present status as full members of God’s household.

The term ἅγιοι (hagioi, saints), then, refers, as it does elsewhere in the letter, to believers without ethnic distinction (1:1, 15, 18; 3:8; 4:12; 5:3; 6:18). Paul is not saying that Gentile believers are now citizens together with Israel (Barth 1974: 66, 269n71) or with Jewish Christians (e.g., E. Scott 1930: 176; Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 71; Faust 1993: 187; Sellin 2008: 233), nor is he imagining that his readers, seated with the enthroned Christ in heaven (2:6), are citizens together with the angels (cf., e.g., Gal. 4:26; Phil. 3:20; Heb. 12:18–24; 1QS 11.7–8; 1QM 12.1–2; 1QHa 11.21–22; Schlier 1957: 140–41; Gnilka 1971: 154). Rather, they form one citizenry with all other believers (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 151; Aletti 2001: 159–60; Hoehner 2002: 392–96). Like them, they are set apart from the rest of the world (1:4; 5:3, 27) as appropriate inhabitants of God’s “holy temple” or “dwelling place” (cf. vv. 21–22). Like them, too, they are “members of [the] household” (οἰκεῖοι, oikeioi) over which God presides as Father (cf. v. 18; 1 Tim. 3:15; 1 Pet. 2:5; Heb. 3:2–6), a thought that forms a skillful contrast with the former plight of Paul’s readers as “resident aliens” (πάροικοι), people who stood outside the “household” that forms God’s society.

[2:20] The idea that his Gentile Christian readers now belong to God’s household leads Paul to shift his metaphor from the social and political realm to the world of architecture. They are part of God’s family, Paul says, because God has incorporated them into a building he has begun to construct on a solid foundation of two elements: apostles and prophets, on one hand, and Christ Jesus himself, on the other. The aorist participle ἐποικοδομηθέντες (epoikodomēthentes) points back in time to the readers’ response to the gospel (1:13) and indicates the cause of what Paul has said in 2:19: his Gentile readers are citizens together with the saints and members of God’s household because they were built on the foundation of the apostles, prophets, and Christ Jesus (Best 1998: 279; Hoehner 2002: 397).[4]

The metaphor of building on a sure foundation was common in classical antiquity and was often used in admonitions or warnings (Plato, Leg. 793b–c; Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.15.8–9]; cf. Soranus, Gynaeciorum 1.47). Here, however, Paul uses the metaphor positively to encourage his Gentile readers that the foundation on which their inclusion in God’s people was built stands firm. This foundation consists of two basic elements, the first with two components.

The first element is οἱ ἀπόστολοι καὶ προφῆται (hoi apostoloi kai prophētai, the apostles and prophets), bound together by a single article (cf. 3:5; Wallace 1996: 270). They form a single foundation because they first proclaimed the gospel to the Gentiles.[5] Does the single article also hint that they are the same people?[6] This seems unlikely since Paul makes a distinction between apostles and prophets in his list of gifts in 4:11 (cf. 1 Cor. 12:28).

They are instead two groups engaged in a common task. The ἀπόστολοι are probably those who first took the gospel to the Gentiles—people such as Barnabas, Timothy, Silvanus, Apollos, and, preeminently, Paul himself (Acts 14:1, 4; 1 Thess. 1:1; 2:7; 1 Cor. 4:6–9; 9:5–6; Rom. 11:13; 15:18–21; Eph. 3:4–9; 1 Tim. 2:7). The προφῆται are not OT prophets,[7] but the same kinds of people Paul refers to in 3:5; 4:11; and 1 Cor. 12:28 (cf. 12:10; 13:2, 8, 9; 14:1–6, 22–40; Rom. 12:6) and who, in those passages, exercise their gifts in the period after Christ’s coming. Such prophets are apparently people whom the Spirit inspires to speak incisively to particular individuals (1 Cor. 14:24–25) or to the church (Acts 11:27–30; 15:32; 21:10–11), especially at critical moments in their lives or in history. Paul may have been thinking here of the role that prophets played in directing the movement of the church outward to the Gentiles (Acts 13:1–3; 15:22, 32; cf. 19:6; Masson 1953: 169–70; Best 1998: 283), a notion that becomes more explicit in 3:5–6, where Paul links the inclusion of the Gentiles with a previously unknown mystery now revealed “by the Spirit to the holy apostles, and prophets.”[8]

The apostles and prophets comprise a foundation whose “most important stone” ἀκρογωνιαίου (akrogōniaiou) is αὐτοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ (autou Christou Iēsou, Jesus Christ himself). The intensification of the name Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς with αὐτός (autos, himself) sets Christ apart from the apostles and prophets as the most important element in the building.[9] This is also the point of ἀκρογωνιαῖος, a rare term that surfaces only in Isa. 28:16 LXX and then, until the second half of the second century, only in a stream of Christian tradition dependent on that text (1 Pet. 2:6; Barn. 6.2–3; Justin, Dial. 114.4; 126.1).

Because the term is so rare, its meaning is not entirely clear. Divided into its two elements, the adjective ἄκρον (akron, “topmost, outermost, inmost”; LSJ 57) and the adjective γωνιαῖος (gōniaios, “on [at] the angle”; LSJ 364), it describes something on or at an extreme corner of a building, either (thinking vertically) at its highest point or (thinking horizontally) at the point most distant from its center. In Isa. 28:16 the adjective is explicitly used to describe a “stone” (λίθος, lithos), a word that in Ephesians we are left to supply from the architectural figure Paul is using. Thus, Christ Jesus could be either a stone that crowns the building at its top when the structure is finished or a stone that is at the foundation’s most distant corner and put in place during the initial phase of construction.

A number of interpreters have taken ἀκρογωνιαῖος in the first sense, as a stone set high in the building and added last. Among their arguments, two considerations weigh heavily. First, the term appears in Symmachus’s Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible (2 Kings 25:17; Ps. 118:22 [117:22 LXX]) and in T. Sol. 22.6–23.4 to refer to an elevated stone.[10] In the Testament of Solomon the stone is placed last in the temple, an image that also makes reasonably good sense in Paul’s own figure, since 2:21–22 reveals that his controlling metaphor is a temple (e.g., Jeremias, TDNT 1:792; 4:275; Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 72; Gnilka 1971: 158; cf. PGL 66).

Second, 4:13–16 recalls the language of harmonious growth present in 2:19–22, but with the human body rather than the construction of a building as the controlling image. In 4:13–16 the church clearly grows up to Christ, who is then immediately identified with the head of the body. The growing building image from 2:19–22 and the growing body image from 4:13–16 would match each other better, it is said, if the stone in one and the head in the other both showed the superiority of the ascended Christ over the whole. This would demand a stone high in the building’s architecture (Lincoln 1990: 155–56; Aletti 2001: 162–63).

Other interpreters have argued compellingly that ἀκρογωνιαῖος must refer to a stone low in the building’s structure, set on top of the foundation and carefully placed to provide guidance and stability for the building’s continuing construction (e.g., McKelvey 1962: 352–59; 1969: 195–204; Schnackenburg 1982: 262–64). This meaning has in its favor consistency with the present tenses that Paul uses in the rest of the figure. As these tenses show, Paul views the building as currently under construction. In this context it makes better sense to think of Christ as providing guidance and stability for this present work than as the “keystone,” placed last and eventually tying everything together (McKelvey 1962: 358–59; Sellin 2008: 239).[11]

In addition, the foundational use of ἀκρογωνιαῖος is more consistent with the use of similar imagery in other relevant literary contexts. In Isa. 28:16, ἀκρογωνιαῖος appears in close proximity to the term θεμέλιος (themelios, foundation) just as it does here, and it refers clearly—even emphatically—to a stone in a building’s foundation.[12] In 1 Cor. 3:11, moreover, Christ is the θεμέλιος of the Corinthian church. He therefore is the critical part of the initial stage of construction just as he is in Eph. 2:20 if ἀκρογωνιαῖος sits low in the building’s structure and provides strength and guidance to all that is built upon it (Schnackenburg 1982: 263–64).

What, then, are we to conclude? The seemingly equal weight of the arguments on either side led one of the greatest modern interpreters of Ephesians, E. Best (1998: 286), to suggest that “in the present state of our knowledge the problem is insoluble” (cf. Lincoln 1990: 155).

It is worth asking, however, whether the interpretive problem arises from too wooden an understanding of the metaphor. Perhaps Paul did not intend ἀκρογωνιαῖος to be understood strictly as either a stone low in the building or as the finishing touch to the building but as both. Mayer (2002: 166) suggests attractively that the author of Ephesians appreciated the ambiguity of the prefixed element ἀκρο-: “Christ as cornerstone is then metaphorically at the same time fundamentum fundamentorum and finis finium.”[13] Paul may have intended the metaphor to show Christ’s importance as anchoring and guiding the growth of the church, which shortly turns out to be the temple and thus to have its foundations, figuratively speaking, in Zion like the ἀκρογωνιαῖος of Isa. 28:16.[14] Paul may have also recognized that this term’s prefixed ἀκρο- allows it to encompass Christ’s role as “head over all things” (1:22–23; cf. 2:6), and his role as the head toward which the body grows (4:13, 15–16). He is, paradoxically, the “topmost foundation stone.”

[2:21] We now learn for the first time that the building Paul has been describing and of which his readers are a part is both a temple and, as the present tense verbs show, presently under construction. Paul develops these thoughts in two subordinate clauses, which are constructed along parallel lines.[15]

Paul first says that Christ Jesus is the person in whom the whole building grows, in a unified way, into a holy temple. The phrase πᾶσα οἰκοδομή would normally be translated “every building,” and some interpreters over the years have rendered it this way (e.g., Lightfoot 1890: 65). This presents a problem, however, since the figure Paul is developing in 2:19–22 seems to assume a single building, not multiple buildings making up a temple complex. As the additional note explains, some early scribes tried to solve the problem by adding the article ἡ in front of οἰκοδομή, thus making Paul refer unambiguously to “the whole building.” Even without the article, however, the phrase can mean this, and the sense demands it.[16] The whole building, then, grows in the sphere encompassed by Christ Jesus.

It also grows συναρμολογουμένη (synarmologoumenē, being joined together). This term appears only here and in 4:16 in all known ancient Greek literature prior to the second century AD.[17] Clearly Paul coined it to match his other συν- (syn-, with) words in chapter 2.﻿[18] Its basic element, ἁρμολογέω (harmologeō) is also rare, but its meaning is not in doubt: it is an architectural word meaning “fit together” or “join” (Maurer, TDNT 7:855), as in the phrase “the beams of the windows are fitted together [ἡρμολόγηται, hērmologētai]” (P.Ryl. 233.6, my trans.; LSJ 244). Paul wants his readers to imagine themselves as part of a building in the process of growing by being tightly fitted together “with” (συν-) other believers across ethnic boundary lines, such as the ones the Mosaic law once imposed (2:14–15).

Paul next reveals that the building he has been talking about all along is ναὸς ἅγιος ἐν κυρίῳ (naos hagios en kyriō, a holy temple in the Lord). Although the imagery would be intelligible in terms of any temple, and Paul’s readers in Roman Asia were surrounded by temples, he was probably thinking specifically of the Jewish temple and, even more specifically, of the role that the temple would play in the days of Israel’s restoration according to Scripture. The way for this has been prepared through his allusion in 2:20 to Isa. 28:16, whose “cornerstone” is laid in Zion, the location of the temple.

That the temple is Israel’s temple is also suggested by Paul’s main theme in 2:11–22 of the inclusion of the Gentiles in the people of God. Isaiah 56:3–8 specifically refers to the inclusion of the nations in temple worship during the period of Israel’s restoration, and as Paul’s allusion to Isa. 57:19 in 2:13 and 17 reveals, he was thinking of this part of Isaiah as he dictated Eph. 2:11–22 (McKelvey 1969: 113; Beale 2004: 259–63; cf. Mayer 2002: 169–72).[19]

The phrase ἐν κυρίῳ refers not to God the Father but to “the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:2–3; Eadie 1883: 203) and means that the location of the temple itself is in the sphere defined by Jesus Christ. Just as the growth takes place “in” him, according to the beginning of 2:21, so the temple exists “in” him. This is a multiethnic temple, the fulfillment of Jewish eschatological expectations, and it is not a physical building: it exists “in the Lord.”

[2:22] Just as in 1:13 (see the comments on that verse), so here, Paul turns directly to his readers with the phrase ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς (en hō kai hymeis, in whom also you). Here too he uses the phrase to apply what he has been saying directly to them. Inasmuch as they are “no longer strangers and aliens” to God’s household but are full members of it, Paul’s Gentile readers are also “being built together” (συνοικοδομεῖσθε, synoikodomeisthe) with other believers into the temple Paul has just described. Like the participle συναρμολογουμένη in 2:21, the verb συνοικοδομεῖσθε is present tense to emphasize that the building is presently under way. It also includes the prefix συν- to communicate that Paul’s readers are being joined “together with” other believers, specifically other Jewish believers since the destruction of the dividing wall of hostility (2:14).[20]

The result of this tightly joined construction, as in 2:21, will be the temple, which Paul now calls κατοικητήριον τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν πνεύματι (katoikētērion tou theou en pneumati, the dwelling place of God in the Spirit). Although κατοικητήριον appears often in the LXX for the dwelling place of people (Exod. 12:20; Pss. 32:14 [33:14 MT, Eng.]; 106:4 [107:4]; Jer. 21:13) or animals (Nah. 2:12 [2:11]; Jer. 9:10 [9:11]; cf. Josephus, Ant. 9.241), it is sometimes used of God’s dwelling place, whether in heaven (1 Kings 8:39, 43, 49; 2 Chron. 6:30, 33, 39; 30:27; 3 Macc. 2:15; cf. Dan. 2:11) or in Zion’s sanctuary (Exod. 15:17 [cf. Philo, Planting 47]; Ps. 75:3 [76:3 MT; 76:2 Eng.]). Paul probably chose this word because of its biblical associations with God’s temple.[21] Just as ναός in 2:21 referred to the temple of the eschatologically restored Israel, so κατοικητήριον also refers to that temple here. Similarly, just as the phrase ἐν κυρίῳ (en kyriō, in the Lord) qualified the noun ναός in 2:21, so here the phrase ἐν πνεύματι qualifies the noun κατοικητήριον to tell us how God dwells within this building: he does so “in” or “by” the Spirit.

This brings Paul’s imagery in 2:19–22 full circle. The household of God (cf. οἰκεῖοι τοῦ θεοῦ, v. 19), into which Paul’s Gentile readers have now been fully integrated, is also the house of God (κατοικητήριον τοῦ θεοῦ, v. 22)—the place where God lives, by his Spirit, with his people.

Summary

In 2:19–22 Paul explores the idea with which he concluded the previous section (v. 18), that Christ had created access for both Jews and Gentiles, as one people, to God the Father. Paul tells his readers that although they are Gentiles, they are fellow citizens with all God’s people. They are members of God’s household and part of the temple in which God’s Spirit dwells. This temple’s foundation is the witness of the apostles and prophets who first went to the Gentiles with the gospel of human reconciliation to God through the death of Christ. The temple’s most important stone—the stone that guides the building’s construction and tops it off when it is finished—is Christ Jesus. Paul’s readers are the carefully shaped and fitted building blocks presently being added to the building. The way in which Paul describes this temple recalls the OT expectation of a rebuilt temple in which Israel and the nations would join together in the worship of God.

This paragraph brings to a close Paul’s effort to explain in greater detail what he meant in 1:19–23 when he said he prayed for God to illuminate the eyes of his readers’ hearts so that they might understand the magnitude of the power he has placed at their disposal in Christ. They had been mired in rebellion against God and alienated from God’s revelation of himself through his people Israel. They were utterly without hope of escape from God’s wrath. Then God, because he is overwhelmingly merciful, saved them and brought them into fellowship with his people, giving them a home in which he is Father, a home that turns out to be the temple where God’s spiritual presence dwells.



Additional Note

2:21. Some ancient witnesses to the text of Ephesians (e.g., אi1, A, C, P, 075, 6, 81, 326, 1739c, 1881, 1912, Chrysostomlem) place ἡ between πᾶσα and οἰκοδομή, dispelling any doubt that Paul is referring to “the whole building” rather than to “every building.” Since the diphthong οἰ and the article ἡ were pronounced in virtually identical ways (Metzger 1968: 191), it is possible that a scribe misheard πᾶσα οἰκοδομή for πᾶσα ἡ οἰκοδομή (Metzger 1994: 534) and so omitted an original ἡ. It is much more likely, however, that a scribe, knowing the expression πᾶσα οἰκοδομή would normally mean “every building,” inserted ἡ to make the meaning “the whole building” explicit and thus preserve the architectural metaphor of a single building. In any case, the correct reading is not in doubt, as the early and geographically widespread attestation of πᾶσα οἰκοδομή without the article reveals (e.g., א*, B, D, F, G, Ψ, 0150, 33, 1739*, 1852, 1962, 2127, 2200, 2464; Hoehner 2002: 407n3; and Metzger 1994: 534).





V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)

VI. Paul’s Divinely Given Task and His Suffering for the Gentiles (3:1–13)

VII. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength and Praises the God Who Can Give It (3:14–21)

VIII. The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)


VI. Paul’s Divinely Given Task and His Suffering for the Gentiles (3:1–13)

In light of his discussion of the inclusion of Gentiles within the household of God in 2:19–22, Paul now begins an intercessory prayer specifically for his readers as Gentiles (3:1). The thought of interceding for Gentiles, however, immediately touches off a digression on his own responsibility to proclaim the gospel to the Gentiles. This digression consumes two paragraphs (3:2–7, 8–13) before Paul returns to his prayer in 3:14, a return he signals by repeating the first two words of 3:1 (τούτου χάριν, toutou charin, on account of this).

The section begins and ends with a reference to Paul’s suffering “for” (ὑπέρ, hyper) his Gentile readers. In 3:1 he is “the prisoner of Christ” for them, and in 3:13 he asks them not to be discouraged about his sufferings for them since these sufferings are their “glory.” In the digression that appears between these two statements, Paul reflects on his “responsibility of administering” (οἰκονομία, oikonomia) the “grace” (χάρις, charis) God has given to him. “Grace” here means the calling he received at the time of his conversion to preach the untraceable riches of Christ to the Gentiles.

The section can be divided into three parts: two brief sentences, one at the beginning and one at the end, and the digression sandwiched between them. The first sentence, never completed, sparks the digression by referring to Paul’s imprisonment in the service of the Gentiles (3:1).

The digression itself consists of two lengthy sentences. The first of these sentences describes the close relationship between the task God has given Paul on behalf of the Gentiles and the mystery God has revealed both to Paul and to “the holy apostles, and prophets” (3:2–7). The second sentence of the digression describes how Paul accomplishes his God-given task (3:8–12).

The section’s final sentence, like its opening sentence, is much shorter than the two sentences that make up the digression. It looks back over the digression and returns to the theme of suffering that initiated it, supplementing it now with a word of encouragement to the letter’s readers (3:13).

This section of the letter bears a number of close verbal, syntactical, and thematic similarities to Col. 1:23–28. Both passages



use the phrase εἴ γε (ei ge, if, as I assume; Col. 1:23; Eph. 3:2)

speak of Paul as ἐγὼ Παῦλος (egō Paulos, I Paul; Col. 1:23; Eph. 3:1)

use the phrase οὗ ἐγενόμην . . . διάκονος (hou egenomēn . . . diakonos, of which I became a servant) to describe the gospel (Col. 1:23; Eph. 3:7)

speak of Paul’s sufferings for his readers (Col. 1:24; Eph. 3:13)

describe Paul’s vocation as an οἰκονομία (oikonomia, administrative responsibility; Col. 1:25; Eph. 3:2)

identify the μυστήριον (mystērion; mystery) with Christ (Col. 1:27; Eph. 3:4)

as something ἀποκεκρυμμένον ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων (apokekrymmenon apo tōn aiōnōn, hidden from eternity; Col. 1:26; Eph. 3:9)

as something now revealed τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ (tois hagiois autou, to his holy people; Col. 1:27) or τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ καὶ προφήταις (tois hagiois apostolois autou kai prophētais, to his holy apostles, and prophets; Eph. 3:5)



To many interpreters the reason for these similarities is clear: the writer of Ephesians was dependent on Colossians, and such dependence is likely only if someone other than Paul wrote Ephesians (e.g., Mitton 1951: 55–97; Lincoln 1990: lv, lxvi–lxviii, 168–70; Sterling 2008: 80–89).

Whoever produced Eph. 3:1–13, however, does not seem to have been paying careful attention to Col. 1:23–28 (pace, e.g., Sterling 2008: 80–89) and appears to have been recalling the language of that letter from memory (cf. Mitton 1951: 55–67, 75). He speaks of Paul’s “sufferings,” for example, as θλίψεσιν (thlipsesin; Eph. 1:13) rather than παθήμασιν (pathēmasin; Col. 1:24), and varies the line τὴν οἰκονομίαν τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν δοθεῖσάν μοι εἰς ὑμᾶς (tēn oikonomian tou theou tēn dotheisan moi eis hymas, the administrative task of God given to me for you; Col. 1:25) so that it becomes the not-quite-identical τὴν οἰκονομίαν τῆς χάριτος τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς δοθείσης μοι εἰς ὑμᾶς (tēn oikonomian tēs charitos tou theou tēs dotheisēs moi eis hymas, the responsibility of administering the grace of God given to me for you; Eph. 3:2).

If we are unwilling to concede that the theological differences between Colossians and Ephesians present an “almost insurmountable difficulty” (Lincoln 1990: lxvii) to the case for the Pauline authorship of Ephesians (see the introduction), then there is no compelling reason to deny that Paul is the author of both Col. 1:23–28 and Eph. 3:1–13. Paul probably dictated this section of Ephesians shortly after composing Colossians, and perhaps because he did so with some emotion, he paid little attention to the niceties of lucid syntax. The author of Ephesians, says Best (1998: 294), “had not cleverly planned what he was going to write.” He began to pray with reference to his imprisonment, digressed to say why he was in prison, and then, reminded by his own digression that he had been on the verge of prayer, decided to go back to the prayer, but not before turning his original reference to his suffering into a word of encouragement for his readers.
